prs.title: feat(streaming): opt-in cap on a streaming response total lifetime (agent.stream_max_lifetime)
prs.body:
You can now set `agent.stream_max_lifetime` to cut a streaming response that keeps sending data but never finishes. It is off by default, so long reasoning streams behave exactly as before unless you turn it on. When a stream is cut, the error names the setting that cut it, and the cut never locks the session out of later requests.

## Before / after (real `hermes chat -q hi`, custom provider pointed at a local server that sends one content chunk every 0.5 s and never finishes; `HERMES_LOCAL_STREAM_STALE_TIMEOUT=10`)

| Leg | Config | Result |
|---|---|---|
| origin/main | `stream_max_lifetime: 15` (key unknown to main) | One request streamed for the whole 130 s run, 0 kills: the stale timer resets on every chunk. |
| `a916290` (before review fixes) | `stream_max_lifetime: 15` | A kill every ~16 s, then `custom rejected the request and retrying won't help … Provider has been unresponsive (no response received) for 6 consecutive stale attempts`. |
| this branch | `stream_max_lifetime: 15` | A kill every ~16 s. Each attempt and the final reply say `Response still streaming after 15s, cut by agent.stream_max_lifetime (15s). Raise agent.stream_max_lifetime, or set it to 0 to turn the cap off, if this model legitimately streams this long.` No breaker line, no "endpoint looks unreachable". |
| this branch, control | key unset (default `0`) | One request streamed for the whole run, 0 kills. Same as main. |

Breaker probe (in-process, real sockets, stale 1 s, cap 1.5 s; two capped calls, then a one-chunk healthy call):

| | `a916290` | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| capped calls | `RemoteProtocolError: stream attempt 3 was superseded`, streak 3 then 6 | `StreamLifetimeExceeded: … cut by agent.stream_max_lifetime (1.5s)`, streak 0 |
| healthy call | `RuntimeError: Provider has been unresponsive … 6 consecutive stale attempts`, **0 requests sent** | OK in 0.1 s |

## Root cause

The stale-stream detector measures the gap since the last chunk and resets on every chunk, so a drip-fed or runaway stream never trips it. Nothing else bounds a stream's total duration on the Chat Completions / Anthropic Messages wire.

## Changes

- `agent/stream_max_lifetime.py`:
  - `resolve_stream_max_lifetime()` reads `agent.stream_max_lifetime`, then the env override `HERMES_STREAM_MAX_LIFETIME`. Default 0 = off. A set value is floored at the effective stale timeout.
  - `StreamLifetime`: a per-call clock that restarts for each new stream attempt and after each kill.
  - `StreamLifetimeExceeded` (a `TimeoutError`, so the attempt is still retried): the error a capped attempt surfaces, naming the setting.
- `agent/chat_completion_stream_monitor.py`: the poll loop calls `_check_stream_lifetime()`, which does nothing when the cap is off. On a cap hit it cancels the attempt, aborts the request-local client and shuts down its socket the way a stale kill does. It marks the attempt as accounted but does **not** count it in the cross-turn stale breaker (`HERMES_STREAM_STALE_GIVEUP`), because the provider was responding. The worker's transport error for that attempt is replaced by `StreamLifetimeExceeded`.
  - If the monitor loop dies unexpectedly, it now logs a stack trace. It also logs the armed stale and cap values at debug level. Both are ported from #100202, co-authored by @krzsda.
- `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py`: `_handle_stream_error` maps a cap-killed attempt's error and treats it as a timeout. Net 0 lines.
- `agent/stream_diag.py`: a cap hit no longer gets the "could not open a stream … endpoint looks unreachable" notice.
- `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py`: `agent.stream_max_lifetime: 0`.
- Docs (configuration and environment-variables): the cap covers Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages streams only. Codex/Responses streams (`codex_responses`, including custom Responses providers) and Bedrock streams are not capped. A cut does not count toward the stale breaker.
- `tests/agent/test_stream_max_lifetime.py`: 2 tests.
  - The drip test drives a real local SSE server through `interruptible_streaming_api_call`. Two capped calls raise `StreamLifetimeExceeded` naming the setting, then a short healthy call succeeds with the breaker set to give up after 2 stale kills. It fails on `a916290` (`RemoteProtocolError: stream attempt 1 was superseded`) and on main (no cap).
  - The other test pins the default (off) and the stale-timeout floor.

Related: #100202 adds a similar always-on absolute cap (`HERMES_STREAM_MAX_SECONDS`, 900 s). This PR differs in three ways: the cap is opt-in, its clock restarts per attempt, and it has a config key and docs. The watchdog logging from #100202 is ported here with credit.

## Tests

`scripts/run_tests.sh` on every test file that touches the stream monitor, `interruptible_streaming_api_call`, stream diagnostics or the stale breaker (40 files): 546 passed, 4 skipped. ruff clean, `scripts/check --only health` 0 blocking, `chat_completion_helpers.py` stays at 4,001 lines.

## Infographic

![infographic](https://v3b.fal.media/files/b/0ab0a46c/2EnFYl_68td9aIpxXWdG__N8vMBZnf.png)

prs.title: fix: two CI races — PTY drain test sleep and a process reaped mid-/proc-probe
prs.body:
## What this fixes

Two CI flakes seen on an unrelated PR's run (job 124674549391), plus one product bug of the same shape found while sweeping.

**1. `test_pty_session.py::test_detach_keeps_draining_into_buffer` — `assert b'one' == b'onetwo'`**

The test slept 50 ms and assumed the PTY drain had by then read `b"one"`, an idle tick and `b"two"`. Each read is a thread-pool round trip (`run_in_executor`), so on a loaded runner only the first had landed. The product is fine: the drain keeps reading while detached. The test was guessing how long three executor hops take.

The tests now wait on what the drain itself publishes: `PtySession.outputs` (chunks read), `alive` (EOF seen) and the viewer's close code. The same 50 ms guess was in three sibling tests (replay-then-live, forced redraw, EOF close), and the base hammer below caught one of them failing on its own (`assert b'hello ' == b'hello world'`). All four now wait on state. PR #73856 tried removing the idle tick from the test data. It was closed because the test had been pruned at the time (it has since come back), and removing the tick only shrinks the window: any fixed sleep still loses to slow enough executor scheduling.

**2. `test_update_custody_tree.py::test_a_killed_owner_takes_the_fetch_helpers_with_it` — `FileNotFoundError: /proc/<pid>/stat`**

`_alive()` sent signal 0, then checked `/proc/<pid>/stat` `exists()`, then `read_text()`. Once the owner is killed the helper is an orphan, and its reaper can collect it between any two of those steps. The read then raised instead of reporting the exit the test was waiting for. The helper now reads the file once and treats `FileNotFoundError` / `ProcessLookupError` as gone (non-Linux keeps the signal-0 answer). The product's `/proc` child scan in `update_custody` already catches `OSError` per entry, so the race is test-only there.

**3. Product, same class: `iron_proxy._pid_alive`**

If the proxy exited between the existence probe and the `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` check, the `exists()` guard skipped the read, `ps -p` then failed, and the function fell through to "if the OS says alive, believe it". A dead proxy then read as alive: `start_proxy` returned early and status showed it running. On Linux a missing `/proc` entry now means gone. Other `OSError`s still fall back to `ps`. New test `test_pid_alive_reads_a_proxy_that_exited_after_the_liveness_probe_as_dead` uses a real `exec -a iron-proxy` process as the alive control, then kills it with the probe pinned true. It is **red on base** (`True`) and green on head.

Swept the rest of the product `/proc` readers (`gateway/status.py`, `update_lock.py`, `_early_recovery.py`, `_subprocess_compat.py`, `web_server_lifecycle.py`, `update_cmd_posix_pause.py`, `dashboard_procs.py`). Each one already reads inside `try` and handles a missing entry. One is left out on purpose: `kanban_db_dispatch._pid_alive`'s zombie peek counts a missing `/proc/<pid>/status` as alive, against its own comment. The next dispatcher tick sees the pid gone, and fake-pid kanban tests depend on that branch, so it is not touched here.

## Evidence

Deterministic injection probes (scratch scripts, not committed):
- PTY: every `FakeBridge.read` takes 30 ms, standing in for a slow executor hop. Base fails `test_detach_keeps_draining_into_buffer`, `test_attach_replays_buffer_then_streams_live` and `test_eof_marks_dead_and_closes_socket_4410`; head passes all four.
- Custody: `Path.read_text` reaps the child just before the stat read. Base raises `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/proc/N/stat'` (CI's exact signature); head returns gone.

Loaded hammer (`flake_hammer.py`: `scripts/run_tests.sh <file>` in a loop beside 2×nproc CPU burners):

| File | Base `c419cf7c864` | Head `0716272f101` |
|---|---|---|
| `test_pty_session.py` | 1 failed of 40 runs (`assert b'hello ' == b'hello world'`) | 0 of 20 |
| `test_update_custody_tree.py` | 0 of 12 | 0 of 12 |

CPU load alone reproduces these rarely (the CI custody failure did not show up in 12 loaded base runs), so the injection probes above are the proof. Each one fails 3 of 3 on base and passes 3 of 3 on head. The iron-proxy race has the same kind of probe: on base, a proxy killed after the liveness probe reads as alive and `ps` runs; on head it reads as gone and `ps` never runs. A live proxy still reads alive on both.

Touched files via `scripts/run_tests.sh` (`test_iron_proxy.py`, `test_iron_proxy_e2e.py`, `test_iron_proxy_cli.py`, `test_pty_session.py`, `test_update_custody_tree.py`): 74 passed, 0 failed, 3 skipped (the e2e file is gated on `HERMES_RUN_E2E=1`). `ruff check` is clean and `scripts/check --only health` is ok.

## Infographic

![two-ci-races-fixed](https://v3b.fal.media/files/b/0ab0a4cf/KkuMtHruvRHoEhEeKafcz_rXVNoQQV.png)

prs.title: Approval cards keep the command and reason after a decision or timeout on Telegram, Feishu and Teams
prs.body:
## Summary Approval cards on Telegram, Feishu and Teams now keep the request (command + reason) after someone taps a button. Before, the card was replaced with just the decision, so a shared chat lost the record of what was approved. A card whose timer runs out now keeps the reason next to the command, and resolved cards no longer say "If you don't answer within 5 minutes it will NOT run". ## Before / after (live: real gateway + real Telegram adapter against the repo's Telegram stand-in) Same scripted turn on each tree: the model asks for `rm -rf …/victim`. In leg 1 the owner taps **Allow once**; in leg 2 nobody answers (`approvals.timeout: 12`). The table shows the last `editMessageText` the adapter sent for the card. The run used a local, uncommitted stand-in patch: the stand-in hands a clicked message back as the raw HTML the bot sent, while Telegram sends plain text plus entities, so for this run the stand-in converted it to text plus entities. | | origin/main | this PR | |---|---|---| | Owner taps Allow once | `✅ Approved once by Tester` (command and reason gone) | `⚠️ Hermes wants to run a command that needs your OK`
`
rm -rf …/victim
`
`Why it was flagged: delete in root path`
`— ✅ Approved once by Tester` (buttons removed) | | Nobody answers | `⌛ Approval timed out after 12 seconds — the command was NOT run. …`
`rm -rf …/victim2` in a code block (reason gone) | `⌛ Approval timed out after 12 seconds — the command was NOT run. …`
`Why it was flagged: delete in root path`
`rm -rf …/victim2` in a code block | ## Changes - **Telegram** (`plugins/platforms/telegram/telegram_resolved_prompt.py`, a new sibling module, so the adapter does not grow): exec-approval and slash-confirm resolutions keep the prompt's own rendering. `Message.text_html` rebuilds it from the entities, so the code block survives. The deadline line is dropped and the decision is added below. If the prompt has no readable body, or Telegram rejects the edit (`BadRequest`, e.g. the extra line pushes it past the length cap), the old decision-only edit runs, so the buttons never stay live. A network error leaves the message as is, since that edit may already have landed. Expired taps keep the body too. - **Feishu**: `_send_exec_approval_prompt` saves the prompt text, minus the deadline line, with the card's state; the replacement card shows it above the decision. The shared card sender just stores whatever extra state it is given, so update-prompt cards are untouched. - **Teams**: the resolved and expired cards show the prompt card's own command preview (up to 2000 chars) instead of a 200-char stub, plus the reason. The adapter keeps that preview in memory under a per-prompt id (last 256 prompts), and each button carries only the id, so the card stays small: a copy per button pushed a long CJK command past Teams' ~28 KB card cap. Cards sent before a restart still read the old `cmd`/`desc` from their button data. The Teams resolved card never showed the deadline line. - **Slack**: the resolved card already kept the body. It now drops the deadline line. - **Timeout edit (every platform that edits its card)**: `gateway/run_turn_runner_approval_settle.py` adds "Why it was flagged" above the command. It is capped at 500 chars, and backtick runs are split as they are in the command. Before, the command was kept but the reason was dropped. ## Other adapters (checked on main) Discord edits only the embed, so the content stays. Its resolved message still shows the deadline line, because removing it means editing the message content as well; that is not part of this PR. Matrix, QQBot, WhatsApp Cloud and relay never edit the prompt. ## Teams card size (real `microsoft-teams-apps` SDK, card built by the adapter and serialized as sent) | command | origin/main | previous head 632178c | this head | |---|---|---|---| | ASCII, 3000 chars | 3,942 B | 11,142 B | 3,170 B | | CJK heredoc, ~2,800 chars | 9,317 B | **30,917 B** (over the ~28 KB cap) | 7,125 B | ## Root cause The resolve handlers built the replacement message from the decision label alone, and the timeout edit built it from the notice plus the command. ## Validation | Check | Result | |---|---| | New/extended tests: Telegram keep-body + overflow fallback + deadline dropped, Telegram network error keeps the prompt, Feishu resolved card, Teams expired tap, Teams full command on the resolved card, Teams button data stays small for a CJK command, timeout edit keeps command + reason | pass; the network-error and Teams-size tests are red on 632178c | | `test_approval_timeout_notice.py`, `test_telegram_approval_buttons.py`, `test_telegram_slash_confirm.py`, `test_feishu_approval_buttons.py`, `test_teams.py`, `test_slack_approval_buttons.py`, `test_discord_approval_lifecycle.py` | 960 passed across the 44 gateway/plugin test files that touch these handlers (incl. these) | | ruff, `check --only health` (no adapter grew; Teams shrank), tmp-literal and windows-footgun checks | clean | Not covered live: Feishu, Teams and Slack. The repo has no stand-in for Feishu or Teams, and this run only drove Telegram. The unit tests above cover all three. Credit: the Feishu half of this bug was first reported with fixes in #10343 (@igangz) and #38363 (@qiushile), both against the pre-plugin `gateway/platforms/feishu.py`. #128983 (@ernani) fixes the Telegram exec-approval half by storing the prompt HTML. ## Infographic ![Approval cards keep their content](https://v3b.fal.media/files/b/0aa5b5bf/XKjOzn2_9W8vnjneEow1E_Ed4eGGYz.png)

prs.title: Approval prompts show hidden Unicode, control bytes and padding instead of hiding them (CLI, gateway, TUI/Desktop)
prs.body:
## Summary
Approval prompts now show everything a command will run. Code points that render as nothing or as a line break become visible escapes on every approval surface. That covers zero-width and bidi characters, variation selectors, the tag block, line/paragraph separators, Braille blank, Hangul fillers and raw control bytes. Padding made of spaces or whitespace-only lines collapses to a marker. Before this, the CLI approval box printed a command with a hidden zero-width character as if the character were not there.

Display-only: the executed command, the smart-approval assessment and the allowlist keys are unchanged. A live run read the tool-call arguments back from `state.db`, and they were byte-identical to the model's raw command.

## Before / after (live: real `hermes chat` in a PTY against a loopback tool-call stub, Allow once)
The model's command was `rm -rf ./build<U+200B>-cache ./x<U+E0100>-y ; echo listing<60×U+2028>; touch PWNED`. The project directory also held two decoy directories, `build-cache` and `x-y`.

| | origin/main | previous head (512fae4) | this head |
|---|---|---|---|
| U+200B | invisible | `\u200b` | `\u200b` |
| U+E0100 (variation selector supplement) | invisible | invisible | `\U000e0100` |
| `; touch PWNED` after 60×U+2028 | hidden behind "… (choose Show full command)" | same, still hidden | `listing⟨\u2028 ×60⟩; touch PWNED` is on screen |
| What ran | the hidden-character directories were deleted, decoys kept, PWNED created | same | same: the `terminal` args in `state.db` == the raw command (116 chars) |

## What it covers
- **Escaped by Unicode category:** every `C*` code point except `\t`/`\n` (control, format, private use, unassigned, surrogate), plus line/paragraph separators (`Zl`/`Zp`).
- **Explicitly listed:** blank-rendering marks and letters from other categories: variation selectors U+FE00–FE0F and U+E0100–E01EF, CGJ, Khmer/Mongolian selectors, Hangul fillers and U+2800. Four or more repeats of one such code point show once with a count: `⟨\u2028 ×300⟩`.
- **Padding:** runs of 21+ spaces/tabs after visible text, ASCII or Unicode (NBSP, U+2000–U+200A, U+3000, …), become ` ⟨+300 whitespace chars⟩ `. So do line-leading runs past 64 characters. 3+ consecutive blank **or whitespace-only** lines become `⟨+N blank lines⟩`, and the line after a collapsed run keeps its indentation.
- **Unchanged:** clean commands, tabs and newlines, normal code indentation, ordinary non-ASCII text (`héllo 日本語 🙂`) and single NBSPs.

## Surfaces
One helper, `agent.redact.redact_approval_display()`, does secret redaction and then `sanitize_command_for_display()`. It is used everywhere an approval string is built:
- the CLI prompt and its callbacks (`tools/approval_prompt.py::_ask_human`, `tools/approval.py::_human_decision`)
- the gateway notify payload and the `execute_code` pending body
- plugin approval transports
- `gateway.run._redact_approval_command`, which feeds messaging buttons and text fallbacks (`gateway/run_turn_runner.py`), TUI/Desktop (`tui_gateway/server.py::_approval_request_payload`), the API server `approval.request` event and pending-control replays.

The command **and the description** are sanitized at those egresses. This means consent prompts (MCP event-subscription instructions, MCP trust gate, vault payment) are covered on gateway, TUI/Desktop and API as well as CLI.

## Root cause
Approval display copies were only secret-redacted. Nothing made hidden characters or padding visible.

## Changes in this round (review follow-up)
- The invisible-character check is now by category (`C*`, `Zl`, `Zp`) plus a short list of blank glyphs. The old fixed allowlist missed U+E0100–E01EF, U+2028/2029, U+2800, U+1BCA0 and U+1D173.
- Whitespace-only lines count as blank lines.
- Runs of one escaped code point collapse to a count.
- Consent descriptions are sanitized on the gateway, TUI/Desktop and API egresses.
- `tui_gateway/server.py` and `gateway/platforms/api_server.py` each shrink by a line.

## Validation
| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `tests/agent/test_approval_display_sanitize.py` | 4 passed. The 2 new invariant tests are red on 512fae4: an all-code-point category sweep plus padding shapes, and consent descriptions on TUI/API |
| Approval/redaction/gateway/TUI/API suites (73 files) | 2437 passed |
| TUI server + approval-event suites after the final edit (22 files) | 1236 passed |
| ruff, `check --only health`, tmp-literal and windows-footgun checks | clean |

Known display limit: padding made of visible characters (for example `"\n\n\n."` repeated) is not collapsed, because collapsing visible lines could hide commands. The CLI modal still offers "Show full command" for it.

Not covered live: Telegram, Discord and Slack buttons, TUI/Desktop and API consent prompts. Those render through the egress functions that the tests drive.

## Infographic

![infographic](https://v3b.fal.media/files/b/0ab0a46e/CzaGSH-VTuojuZooqnv7M_SumJl9ZM.png)

prs.title: fix(middleware): tool_request middleware sees the model's pre-Relay call as original_args
prs.body:
`tool_request` middleware now gets the model's own tool call as `original_args`, even when Relay rewrote the call first, matching what `tool_execution` middleware already sees.

## What changed in this rebase
The original scope of this PR (salvage of #73656 by @cresslank) was sequential chaining of request-middleware rewrites. That landed on main in #133159 (f67d490f71c), so the salvaged commit resolved to empty and is dropped; credit to @cresslank stands for the design. Main deliberately gives each callback its own payload copy (`test_request_middleware_in_place_mutation_does_not_leak`), so the in-place-mutation compatibility idea from the thread is not taken.

The one piece still missing on main is kept:

| Situation | `original_args` a `tool_request` middleware sees — main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Relay rewrote `{"path": "a"}` → `{"path": "b"}` | `{"path": "b"}` (Relay's output) | `{"path": "a"}` (model's call) |
| No Relay rewrite | args | args (unchanged) |

- `agent/tool_executor.py`: pass `function_args` as `original_args` when Relay args are fed in.
- `hermes_cli/middleware.py`: `apply_tool_request_middleware(..., original_args=None)` keyword; default keeps old behaviour.
- One invariant test in `tests/hermes_cli/test_plugins_middleware_chain.py` (red on main).

Root cause: the snapshot was taken from the already-Relay-rewritten args.

Not covered live: the Relay leg needs an active Relay intercept session; covered by the unit test.

prs.title: fix(kanban): kanban_task_blocked fires after commit for dependency waits (salvage #81339)
prs.body:
A Kanban plugin hooked on `kanban_task_blocked` can now read and write the board when a task enters a dependency wait. Before, it saw stale state and stalled on its own caller's SQLite write lock.

Fixes #145885. Salvage of #81339 by Marc D'Aoust, with authorship kept on the fix commit.

## Before / after (real `hermes kanban` CLI, scratch `HERMES_HOME`, real plugin)

This was a dependency chain built with the CLI: `create` parent → `create` child → `link` → child back in `ready` → `kanban block <child> --kind dependency`. A plugin registered `kanban_task_blocked`. In the hook it opened a second connection, read the task, and ran `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` plus a comment insert, with a 2 s busy timeout.

| | origin/main `c419cf7` | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| status the observer reads | `ready` (uncommitted, stale) | `todo` (committed) |
| observer's board write | `FAILED: database is locked` after 2.01 s | `ok` in 0.01 s |
| `kanban block` wall time | 3.84 s (stalled for the full busy timeout) | 1.35 s |
| control: `--kind needs_input` | `blocked`, write ok | `blocked`, write ok |

With the default busy timeout, a real plugin's write retries for minutes before it gives up. Issue #145885 measured about 720 s of board-wide stall.

## Root cause
`block_task` fired `kanban_task_blocked` for `kind="dependency"` inside its `write_txn`. Every other block kind fires after commit, and the docs promised post-commit for all of them. The in-txn branch was carried forward as "historical ordering" by an AST-neutral refactor and was never a design choice.

## Changes
- `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py`: dropped the dependency-only in-transaction dispatch (−4 lines). It now uses the shared post-commit dispatch. The payload is unchanged, and the task snapshot is still taken inside the transaction.
- `tests/hermes_cli/test_kanban_lifecycle_hooks.py`: added one invariant test, parametrized as dependency plus a needs_input control. During the hook, a second connection sees the committed status and event and can take the write lock.
- `website/docs/user-guide/features/hooks.md` (+ zh-Hans): removed the "dependency-wait fires before its transaction exits" caveat.

## What changed in this rebase
- Rebuilt on current main. `block_task` has been refactored since (`_route_block`, the module split), so the original +183/−94 re-indent became a 4-line deletion.
- Trimmed the 1,263-line, 17-test file to the one invariant. It now lives in the existing lifecycle-hooks test file.
- Updated the docs that described the old ordering.
- Swept the same class of bug: an AST scan of every `hermes_cli/kanban*.py` on main found no other lifecycle hook call inside a `write_txn`.

## Validation
| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| New test on origin/main | dependency case red: `('ready', 'linked', 'database is locked') != ('todo', 'dependency_wait', 'free')`; control green |
| New test on head | 4/4 passed |
| Related suites (block_kinds, kanban_db, lifecycle_hooks, review_lifecycle_complete) | 86 passed, 1 skipped |
| ruff, `scripts/check --only health`, tmp-literals, windows-footguns, attribution | pass |

## Infographic

prs.title: fix(agent): name the phase and the setting in transport-timeout error summaries
prs.body:
A provider timeout that exhausts the retries now tells you whether the connection was ever made and which setting to raise, instead of the SDK's bare "Request timed out." / "timed out".

## Before / after (real `hermes chat -q hi`, custom provider pointed at a local socket server that accepts and never answers; `HERMES_API_TIMEOUT=6`, `agent.auto_recovery_cycles: 0`)

| | origin/main `c419cf7c864` | this branch (`c15587cf2f8`) |
|---|---|---|
| Per-attempt line | `⚠️  Attempt 1/3 failed: Request timed out.` | `⚠️  Attempt 1/3 failed: Request timed out waiting for the provider to respond (if the model needs longer, raise providers.custom.request_timeout_seconds in config.yaml)` |
| Terminal line | `❌ API failed after 3 retries — Request timed out.` | `❌ API failed after 3 retries — Request timed out waiting for the provider to respond (if the model needs longer, raise providers.custom.request_timeout_seconds in config.yaml)` |
| Chat reply | `Provider said: Request timed out.` | `Provider said: Request timed out waiting for the provider to respond (…)` |
| Connect timeout (openai `APITimeoutError` caused by `httpx.ConnectTimeout`) | `Request timed out.` | `Connection to the provider timed out before it was established (check the base_url and network path)` |
| Pool / write timeout (provider never got to answer) | `Request timed out.` | unchanged |
| An HTTP error raised inside an `except ReadTimeout:` handler (e.g. 401) | `HTTP 401: Invalid API key` | unchanged |
| Any non-timeout error | unchanged | unchanged |

The connect row is from the unit test with real httpx/openai exception objects; a live connect-timeout run (base_url on a non-routable IP) ends on the stale-stream breaker before the connect timer, on both trees.

## Root cause

`ApiErrorSummaryMixin._summarize_api_error` had no timeout case, so a timeout fell through to `str(error)`. The openai SDK wraps every httpx timeout, connect included, in `APITimeoutError("Request timed out.")`, so the phase is only visible in the cause chain.

## Changes

- `agent/timeout_error_summary.py` (new): reads the phase from the explicit `__cause__` chain only (the SDK's `raise APITimeoutError(...) from err`; `__context__` is a different failure) and returns one line per phase, or `None` for anything else, including pool and write timeouts. The read-phase hint names the agent's real provider key (`providers.<agent.provider>.…`); a class-level call keeps the `<provider>` placeholder. Both lines keep the "timed out" wording that the cron failure notice and the error classifier match on.
- `agent/api_error_summary.py`: `_summarize_api_error` consults it right after the offline (DNS) check. A small descriptor passes `provider=agent.provider` when it is called on an agent; every caller and one-argument test stub keeps the `(error)` call shape.
- `tests/agent/test_timeout_error_summary.py`: 5 tests. The phase test fails on origin/main; the three review-fix tests (pool/write keep the old text, a 401 raised inside a timeout handler keeps `HTTP 401`, the hint names the agent's provider) fail on `8a43794c067` and pass on `c15587cf2f8`.

## What changed in this rebase

- `_summarize_api_error` moved from `run_agent.py` to `agent/api_error_summary.py`, and its callers from `agent/conversation_loop.py` to `agent/turn_recovery.py`. The fix now lives only in the summary module: no `run_agent.py` / `conversation_loop.py` / `turn_recovery.py` hunks. The old `provider`/`model` keyword arguments are gone because several existing tests stub `_summarize_api_error(self, error)` with one argument.
- The old body said the summary was blank. With the current httpx/openai that's no longer true (`str()` is "Request timed out." / "timed out"), so the PR now improves a vague message rather than filling an empty one.
- The phase check now follows the cause chain. Matching on the outer type name alone reported every SDK-wrapped connect timeout as a read timeout.

prs.title: fix(background-review): memory review saves only grounded facts, not guesses
prs.body:
## Summary
The background memory review now saves only facts the conversation actually supports. On current main it turns a one-off "make that shorter" into a permanent "User prefers concise responses" and files passing remarks as profile entries. With this change those guesses go away, and explicitly stated facts and environment facts are still saved.

Root cause: the memory routing block shared by `_MEMORY_REVIEW_PROMPT` and `_COMBINED_REVIEW_PROMPT` tells the fork *where* to save but gives no rule for *what* counts as a fact.

## Live A/B (real review path, current prompts)
`spawn_background_review_thread(..., review_memory=True)` → real `build_cache_parity_fork` → real memory tool writes into a scratch `HERMES_HOME`. Generator: `meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct` (a weak model, on purpose). Four fixed transcripts, 3 reps on main and 3 on head. The table lists what ended up in USER.md / MEMORY.md:

| Transcript | main (`c419cf7`) | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| One-off "make that one shorter, it's for slack" | 3/3 saved "User prefers concise responses" | 0/3 (nothing saved) |
| Beginner questions mentioning a kid's science fair | 3/3 saved "Has a kid with a science fair project" (+ matplotlib trivia 1/3) | 0/3 |
| Control: "I'm based in Berlin… from now on always Celsius and km. Remember that." | 3/3 saved | 3/3 saved |
| Control: env facts found while debugging (docker group, compose v1 path) | 3/3 → MEMORY.md | 3/3 → MEMORY.md |

A first draft scoped the rule to USER.md only. In that draft the "prefers concise responses" guess just moved to MEMORY.md (2/2), so the rule is store-neutral: it accepts a user message **or a tool result** as evidence, which keeps environment facts flowing into MEMORY.md.

## Changes
- `agent/background_review.py`: adds one sentence block to `_MEMORY_ROUTING_BLOCK`. A fact must be grounded in a user message or tool result; no inferring traits, skill level, role, mood or preferences from topic, tone or tools; no promoting a one-off request to a standing preference unless the user marked it general or stated a standing like/dislike ('I hate X', 'stop doing Y'); if unsure, leave it out. The memory-only and combined prompts both get it, and the skill-only prompt stays the same.
- Cost: **~113 tokens** (95 for the rule, +18 for the like/dislike clause added in review) per memory or combined review run. It goes into the fork's user message only, not the system prompt or `tools[]`, so `tests/fixtures/prompt_surface/` is unchanged and no hermes-agent-core prompt-surface approval is needed.
- `tests/agent/test_memory_review_grounding.py`: one invariant test (the rule is in both memory-bearing prompts and absent from the skill prompt). It fails on main.

## Review fix (`507634d54ad`)
The rule's examples of a general preference ('always', 'from now on', 'remember') could be read as a required keyword list, so the review asked that a stated like or dislike count too. Component probe (transcript + each tree's `_MEMORY_REVIEW_PROMPT` + a `memory` tool, Nous `/chat/completions`, `google/gemini-3.8-flash`, temperature 0.7):

| Transcript | main | PR before fix (`f4eb3c4`) | this head (`507634d`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| "ugh, stop putting emojis in everything, I hate that. redo it." (real `MEMORY_SCHEMA`) | 11/11 saved | 11/11 | 11/11 |
| same, minimal tool schema | 11/11 | 11/11 | 11/11 |
| One-off "make that one shorter, it's for slack" | 0/5 saved | 0/5 | 0/5 |
| Prompt tokens (emoji, real schema) | 804 | 899 | 917 |

The review's run had the PR at 8/11 on the emoji case; these runs did not reproduce that drop at this sample size. The clause still removes the keyword-list reading for +18 tokens and does not make the one-off "shorter" request stick.

## Rebased onto current main
Main rewrote these prompts (two-store USER.md/MEMORY.md routing, #30220) after this PR was opened. The original rule said "every entry must trace to a specific user message", which would have blocked MEMORY.md environment facts that come from tool output. I rebuilt it on the new structure, cut it to about half its original length, and made it store-neutral.

Tests: 53/53 passed across the new test plus `test_background_review*.py`, `test_refine_focus.py`, `test_prompt_surface.py` and `test_session_memory_review.py`. ruff, `scripts/check --only health`, tmp-literal and windows-footgun checks are clean.

prs.title: feat(slack): show emoji reactions in thread context so reacted-to messages read as answered
prs.body:
## Summary

When the agent is mentioned in a Slack thread, the thread context it reads now includes each message's emoji reactions. A message answered with 12 :white_check_mark: and no replies no longer reads as "nobody responded".

Read-side only: this does not route live `reaction_added` events to the agent (#10583). Opt-in reaction triggers already exist on main (#70195).

## Before / after (real gateway run)

A real `hermes gateway run` was driven through the real `plugins/platforms/slack` adapter. A local Slack stand-in served the Web API and Socket Mode websocket, and the model was `anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5` on Nous. The thread root asks people to react ✅ to sign off and carries 12 ✅ and 1 👀. The user asks: "how many people signed off on the root message? Answer with just the number, or 'unknown'".

| Leg | Thread-context root line the agent received (read from the run's `state.db`) | Reply posted to Slack |
|---|---|---|
| `origin/main` c419cf7 | `[thread parent] Ana: Staging deploy 4.12 looks clean… safe to promote to prod.` | `unknown` |
| this PR | `[thread parent] Ana: Staging deploy 4.12 looks clean… safe to promote to prod. [reactions: :white_check_mark:×12 :eyes:]` | `12` |
| this PR, same thread with no reactions (control) | byte-identical to main's line | `unknown` |
| this PR, allowlist = asker only (trust) | `[thread parent] [unverified] Ana: … [reactions: :white_check_mark:×12 :eyes:]`. The header still tells the model not to act on `[unverified]` lines. | `12` |

Every leg made exactly one `conversations.replies` call per turn, so there are no extra Slack API calls.

**Root cause:** `_format_thread_context` rendered text, blocks, attachments and file markers but ignored the `reactions` array that `conversations.replies` already returns.

## Changes

- `plugins/platforms/slack/adapter_reactions_context.py` (new sibling): `slack_reactions_marker(msg)` → `[reactions: :name:×count …]`.
  - Lists at most 8 distinct emoji, then `+N more`.
  - `count` is used because Slack truncates `users`.
  - Names are reduced to Slack's emoji-name charset, so a crafted name cannot add newlines or brackets.
- `adapter.py::_format_thread_context` appends the marker to each context line, on the same line, so it keeps that line's `[unverified]` trust tag.
- It is kept out of `parent_text`, which drives mention wake checks.
- `tests/gateway/test_slack_reaction_context.py`: 2 invariant tests through `_fetch_thread_context` (marker placement, cap and `parent_text` left unchanged; a hostile name cannot forge context structure). Both fail on `origin/main` and pass here.

## What changed in this rebase

- Rebuilt on current `origin/main`. `adapter.py` is now 6,950 lines, so the helper moved out of the facade into a sibling; the facade only gains the call site.
- The marker is applied only to thread-context lines, not inside `_render_message_text`, so the parent-text fetch used for mention wake checks is unchanged.
- The test file was trimmed from 7 helper-level tests to 2 invariants that go through the real context path.
- Upstream provenance was removed from the code, commit and title.

## Validation

- `scripts/run_tests.sh` over the new file plus 9 Slack thread-context suites: 270 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
- ruff, `scripts/check --only health`, `check_no_tmp_literals`, `check-windows-footguns --all` and `audit_pr_attribution`: all clean.
- The live legs above used a real gateway process, real adapter and real model (~$0.01). Only Slack itself was a local stand-in.

prs.title: Cron jobs know what time they fired: run time in every scheduled prompt
prs.body:
Scheduled cron jobs now know what time they fired: every run's prompt carries `[CURRENT RUN TIME: <weekday, date HH:MM zone> (UTC±hh:mm)]` in the configured timezone.

## What changes (real runs, `google/gemini-3.8-flash`, prompt read back from the run's `state.db`)

Job prompt: *"Reply with ONE line: the exact current run time you were given in this prompt (copy it verbatim), or the word NONE if no time-of-day was given to you. Do not call any tools."*

| Leg | User message the job sent | Model's reply |
|---|---|---|
| `origin/main`, `hermes cron run` | hint + prompt, no time of day | `NONE` |
| this PR, `hermes cron run` (America/Los_Angeles) | `[CURRENT RUN TIME: Saturday, 2026-10-31 14:57 PDT (UTC-07:00)]` | `Saturday, 2026-10-31 14:57 PDT (UTC-07:00)` |
| this PR, real scheduler tick inside `gateway run` (`timezone: Asia/Tokyo`) | `[CURRENT RUN TIME: Sunday, 2026-11-01 06:59 JST (UTC+09:00)]` | `Sunday, 2026-11-01 06:59 JST (UTC+09:00)` |

Root cause: the system prompt carries only `Conversation started: <day>` (date-only, kept byte-stable for prompt caching), so a 07:00 morning brief could not tell itself from a 19:00 retry, and time-stamped reports invented times or spent a tool call on `date`.

## Changes
- `cron/scheduler_prompt.py`: `_run_time_line()` renders `hermes_time.now()` (configured zone, else server-local) through `safe_strftime`; `_build_job_prompt` puts it right after `_CRON_HINT`. The hint constant stays byte-identical.
- `tests/cron/test_cron_run_time.py`: 2 tests (line placed between hint and job prompt; survives the skill-assembly path), both red on `origin/main`.

## Prompt-cache impact
- System prompt untouched.
- Skill-backed jobs: the line sits in the per-run volatile part after the registered stable skill prefix (#81867), so the cross-run skill scaffold cache is unchanged (`tests/agent/test_prompt_cache_boundary.py` passes).
- Cron sessions are fresh per fire, so no past message is ever rewritten. Cost: ~25 tokens per run.

## This rebase
- `_build_job_prompt` moved from `cron/scheduler.py` (now 4.4k lines) into `cron/scheduler_prompt.py` since this PR was opened; the change now lives there and `cron/scheduler.py` is untouched.
- The line is now its own bracketed line rather than an edit inside the hint text, so the hint stays byte-stable and open hint-wording PRs (e.g. #138737) don't conflict.
- Added the UTC offset (so `%Z` abbreviations are unambiguous) and moved tests out of the 2.6k-line `test_scheduler.py` into a 2-test file with a fixed clock.
- Commit message no longer names the source project.

## Validation
- `tests/cron/test_cron_run_time.py`, `test_scheduler.py`, `test_cron_prompt_injection_skill.py`, `test_notepad.py`, `test_cron_script.py`, `tests/agent/test_prompt_cache_boundary.py`: 200 passed, 1 skipped (Windows-only).
- `scripts/check --only health`, tmp-literal, Windows-footgun and attribution checks: clean.

prs.title: test(cron): profile-timezone test no longer fails the day before a DST change
prs.body:
Today's PR CI fails `tests/cron/test_cron_next_run_profile_timezone.py`. It is a test-only date bug, not a cron bug.

## Cause
The test checks that a `0 14 * * *` job in an America/New_York profile is saved with New York's UTC offset. It compared the saved offset against New York's offset *today*. On Oct 31 (EDT, -04:00), the next 14:00 run is Nov 1, after DST ends (EST, -05:00). The scheduler correctly saved `2026-11-01T14:00:00-05:00`, and the test flagged it as a foreign offset.

Example failure: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/actions/runs/41245623830/job/124668652602 (on unrelated PR #147341). Main's last push run, from 10:03 UTC, was green; the test turned red once the next run crossed the DST change. It would recur around every DST change.

## Change
The expected offset is now New York's offset at `next_run` itself. The invariant still holds: a job saved with the backend's UTC offset (`14:00+00:00`) still fails, since New York is never +00:00.

## Verification
`HERMES_TEST_FILE_RETRIES=0 scripts/run_tests.sh tests/cron/test_cron_next_run_profile_timezone.py` on Oct 31 21:xx UTC:

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|

prs.title: fix(checkpoints): prune preview and execution agree on orphan detection
prs.body:
Fixes the divergence where `hermes checkpoints prune` previews orphans it then refuses to delete.

- **One verdict for preview and execution.** `store_status()` exposes `orphan_confirmable` and the prune preview filters on it — for v2 store records and for pre-v2 shadow repos. For pre-v2 shadow repos an unreadable marker or a blank workdir is never confirmable (only an unset `None` workdir is); v2 records with a missing or blank workdir keep their pre-existing "confirmable" treatment, which is unchanged here.
- **A vanished parent directory is not deletion evidence.** `st_dev` equality with a surviving ancestor does not prove the *parent* was deleted (a removed mount point or a volume remounted under a new name produces the same shape), so those restore points are preserved — consistent with `test_absent_workdir_without_deletion_evidence_keeps_history`.
- **Silence replaced by reporting.** `checkpoints status` lists unreachable records with the reason prune skips them (`parent path gone; deletion not corroborated (conservative)`, `volume identity drift: recorded parent_dev …`, `parent directory reborn on a different identity: …`) plus a separate `Pre-v2 shadow repos (N):` section that falls back to the shadow repo path when the recorded workdir is blank or missing.
- **The destructive prompt names what it deletes.** Pre-v2 orphans without a recorded workdir show their shadow repo path, v2 orphans show `checkpoint <hash>`. `(unknown)` is gone; the only remaining placeholder is `(no recorded identity)`, which is defensive-only — the store always writes a hash (the meta file name stem), so it never mislabels a real record.

Closes #147154

prs.title: test(gateway): wait for the dropped viewer's fanout writer in the reconnect-gap test
prs.body:
## Summary

Deflakes `tests/gateway/test_authority_reconnect_gap.py::test_resume_after_replay_delivers_the_frames_published_in_between`, which went red in CI on an unrelated PR (#147362):

```
assert replay['events'] == []
AssertionError: Left contains 2 more items, first extra item: {... 'type': 'message.complete', 'seq': 4 ...}
```

## Root cause: test synchronisation, not a product race

The test takes the dropped viewer's replay cursor as "the last frame in its queue" right after the turn's drain task finishes. The session fanout (`tui_gateway.transport.FanoutTransport`) hands frames to each subscribed peer on that peer's own daemon writer thread. So a turn can finish with its `message.complete` (seq 4) and idle `session.info` (seq 5) already published to the replay ring but not yet handed to the peer. On a loaded runner the test read cursor 3, and `session.events.since(3)` correctly answered with frames 4 and 5, not the empty list the test expected.

**Why this isn't a product bug:** both frames are committed to the ring before the drain task ends (`commit_and_publish` publishes under `event_stream.lock` inside the drain's awaited settlement). A real client whose socket only saw seq 3 gets 4 and 5 back from the replay, exactly as this failure shows. Nothing is lost or duplicated. The reconnect fix this test guards (f57628bcb20, `SessionEvents.catch_up` in `attach`) writes synchronously under the stream lock before the transport joins the fanout, so the rest of the test was already deterministic.

## Fix

The test now waits on the dropped peer's queue until the frame at the stream's published watermark arrives (`_receive_through`, run off the loop with `asyncio.to_thread`), then asserts the cursor equals that watermark. The `queue.get(timeout=30)` only limits how long a real hang can block. It is not a sleep and it doesn't widen any timeout. No production code changes.

## Repro / verification

| leg | result |
|---|---|
| origin/main, `flake_hammer.py` (2×nproc CPU burners), 40 runs | **2/40 FAILED**, same assertion (e.g. `Left contains one more item: ... session.info`) |
| origin/main + 0.2 s delay injected at top of `FanoutTransport._drain` | **FAILED**, same signature as CI (`Left contains 2 more items ... message.complete`) |
| this branch + same injected delay | passed |
| this branch, `catch_up` call in `attach` neutralised (mutant) | **FAILED** (`assert ([])`): the test still guards f57628bcb20 |
| this branch, `flake_hammer.py` (2×nproc CPU burners), 25 runs | 25/25 passed |
| `scripts/check --only health`, ruff | ok |

Sweep: no existing PR or issue matches the test name, the file name or the symptom.

prs.title: test(telemetry): settle the export worker before engagement assertions read the store
prs.body:
## What

`tests/hermes_cli/test_shared_metrics_engagement.py::test_a_closed_day_reports_active_time_surfaces_and_primary_model_once` failed once in CI (unrelated PR #80873, run on 2026-11-01 ~04:10 UTC) with `assert [] == [(cli 5m_to_30m, 1), (gateway lt_5m, 1)]` right after the test moved its clock to the next day. A retry passed.

## Root cause

It was test isolation. The clock and time zone were not involved.

- Each finished turn starts the background `hermes-shared-metrics-flush` worker. That worker opens its own write transactions on the profile's metrics store.
- A user-path write that hits one of those transactions after the 250 ms busy timeout gets **deferred in memory** until that store's next write. This is intended (`SharedMetricsStore._write_or_defer`).
- The file's `_flush()` helper only called the fake Relay's `subscribers.flush()`, which does nothing. So an assertion could read the store while the day-closing writes (the other process's `engagement.record` and the `cli-2` turn) were still sitting in the deferred queue. The closed day then looked unreported: `[]`.

Ruled out: the file passes with the whole process clock moved (time-machine) to 2026-10-26, 10-27, 10-28, 10-31 and 2026-11-01T04:10Z, and also with `TZ=America/Los_Angeles`. The `Relay plugin initialization failed: '_Relay' object has no attribute 'plugin'` warning in the CI log is printed by passing runs too.

## Fix (test only)

`_flush()` now joins the export worker, using the runtime suite's existing `_join_export_workers`. It then drains deferred writes on every runtime store and on any store the test passes in; the closed-day test passes its second-process store. No product change and no sleeps.

## Verification

- **Deterministic repro.** A scratch probe starts a thread named like the export worker. It holds the store's write transaction while the next day's interactions arrive, then lets go. That is the same shape as a slow export pass on a loaded runner.
  - base `origin/main`: **0/7 pass**. Each failure is exactly the CI assertion, `assert [] == [('{"active_m...ateway"}', 1)]`.
  - head: **7/7 pass**.
- **Probabilistic repro.** Every write transaction the worker opens is slowed by +0.3 s. Base hit the CI assertion 1 time in 23 runs; head passed 15/15.
- `test_shared_metrics_engagement.py` plus `test_relay_shared_metrics_runtime.py`: 72 passed, both at the real date and with the clock moved to 2026-11-01T04:10Z.
- `flake_hammer.py` (CPU-saturated loop through `scripts/run_tests.sh`) on head: 10/10 runs, 0 fails.
- `scripts/check --only health` ok; ruff clean.

prs.title: fix(providers): resolve the named-custom-provider profile instead of the billing class
prs.body:
## Thinking Path

- A named custom provider defined in `config.yaml`'s `providers:` section resolves at runtime to the bare billing class `custom` (`_custom_runtime()` in `hermes_cli/runtime_provider_custom.py` builds `rp._runtime("custom", ...)` regardless of the requested slug).
- `agent_init` then sets `agent.provider = "custom"`, so `get_provider_profile(agent.provider)` in `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py` lands on the bundled Ollama-leaning `CustomProfile`.
- Any per-provider quirk that profile carries is silently applied to providers that reject it. Concrete symptom: a provider that requires thinking replies with HTTP 400 `REASONING_REQUIRED` because the generic profile injects an Ollama-style `extra_body.think`.
- `agent.requested_provider` carries the persistent config slug through the billing-class rewrite, so a one-shot retry with it resolves the provider's own profile.

## What Changed

- `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py`: the profile lookup is factored into a module-level resolver with a named-custom fallback — when the resolved profile is missing or is the generic `CustomProfile`, retry once with `agent.requested_provider` (ignored when it is `"custom"` itself).
- Registered non-custom providers and bare-custom-without-a-named-entry keep today's behaviour; nothing changes for anyone not hitting the mismatch.
- Added `tests/agent/test_custom_provider_profile_fallback.py` (4 tests): named slug wins, no requested slug keeps the generic profile, registered providers are never overridden even with a stale requested slug, `requested_provider="custom"` is ignored.

## Verification

prs.title: fix(pm): name the failure uv hit, not the tail of its log
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

`classify_uv_failure` reported **the last 600 characters of uv's output** as the reason a `uv sync`/`uv lock` failed. For a failed sdist build those characters are the build backend's own output, which runs last — and setuptools ends it with a held-back `SetuptoolsDeprecationWarning` about license classifiers. The line that actually stopped the build (a missing `clang++`) sits above it, so the reason a user was handed was:

```
… uv sync exited 1: License classifiers are deprecated. … Apache Software License
```

This PR names the failure instead: the last line that reports one, with uv's own `Failed to build <package>` header above it, falling back to the bounded tail only when no line does.

```
uv sync exited 1:   x Failed to build `python-olm==3.2.16`
error: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'clang++'
```

Nothing about the classification changes — resolver conflicts, undated-index failures and bytecode-compile handling are decided from the full output exactly as before; only the text of `cause` is built differently.

## Related Issue

Refs #132820

This is the diagnosis half of that issue. The report is right that a failing optional extra aborts the whole update, but the reason it was unreadable is this bug: the PM warning hid the real error behind a license notice, which is what sent people looking at the wrong thing. Making an optional extra's build failure *not* fail `hermes update` means a per-extra build and a package→extra map PM does not have today (uv reports `python-olm`, not `matrix`), so it is a design change for a maintainer to make rather than a drive-by fix; this PR removes the wrong-reason obstacle in front of it.

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)

## Changes Made

- `pm/environment.py`: `_failure_reason(output)` — the last line matching a failure marker (`error:`, `fatal error`, `cmake error`, `no such file or directory`, `failed with exit status`), prefixed with the last `failed to build` header when uv printed one, bounded to 600 chars; `output.strip()[-600:]` remains the fallback. `classify_uv_failure` uses it for `cause`.
- `tests/pm/test_workspace.py`: `test_failed_build_names_the_error_not_the_warning_after_it` (the python-olm-shaped log above) and `test_failure_without_a_named_line_keeps_the_bounded_tail` (the fallback still keeps the diagnostics the streamed capture exists for).

## How to Test

1. `python -m pytest tests/pm/test_workspace.py -q` → `10 passed`.
2. Red on the base: with only `pm/environment.py` reverted, `test_failed_build_names_the_error_not_the_warning_after_it` fails at
   `assert '              Apache Software License'.endswith("No such file or directory: 'clang++'")` — i.e. the bug is the assertion, not the fixture.
3. `python scripts/check --base HEAD~1` → `scripts/check: 12 checks, ok` (0 blocking, 0 advisory).

prs.title: fix(tools): bound a check_fn probe so a wedged availability check cannot hang the turn
prs.body:
## The problem

A `check_fn` probes external state (a Docker daemon, an MCP server, a browser control endpoint). The probe ran inline on the caller's thread, so a probe that never returned held its caller forever.

Two call sites, both on a turn's critical path:

- the boot warm-up — `gateway/run.py::_warm_turn_machinery_sync` → `model_tools.get_tool_definitions()` → `registry.get_definitions()` → the probe sweep
- the first inbound turn — `agent/agent_init.py::_load_tools` → the same build

#131145 reports the result: a boot whose warm-up never finished (`Turn-machinery warm-up still running after 20s; opening inbound gate anyway`) left the **first** inbound turn wedged forever. The agent was constructed, the tool `check_fn`s ran, and then the turn stopped dead **before issuing any provider request**:

```
tools.registry: check_fn _browser_cdp_check returned False; dependent tools will be unavailable this turn
tools.registry: check_fn _browser_dialog_check returned False; dependent tools will be unavailable this turn
tools.registry: check_fn is_browser_use_cli_mode returned False; dependent tools will be unavailable this turn
<no further lines, ever>
```

Nothing was logged, nothing was surfaced, `active_agents` stayed at `1`, and the messaging platform kept showing "typing" until a gateway restart. The probe that never answered was the one after those three verdicts.

The probe was unbounded, so nothing downstream could recover: the warm-up only logs `WARNING` and continues in the background, and the turn's inactivity watchdog waits `agent.gateway_timeout` (1800 s by default).

## The fix

The probe now runs on a worker thread with a **10 s budget** (the environment probe's budget — `tools/env_probe.py::_PROBE_WAIT_TIMEOUT`, healthy runtime ~0.5 s). A probe that cannot answer within it counts as "not available" instead of hanging the turn, and says so:

```
WARNING tools.registry: check_fn check_x_requirements did not answer within 10.0s;
        dependent tools will be unavailable this turn
```

Properties that had to survive the change:

- **The profile scope still resolves inside the probe.** The worker runs under the caller's contextvars (`spawn_context_thread`), so the profile secret scope and the Hermes-home override still resolve in the probe. Without this, every scoped probe would fail closed and strip its toolset (#110635).
- **The probe's own contextvar writes still reach the caller.** The memory tool publishes its availability snapshot from the `check_fn` for the `dynamic_schema_overrides` call that follows it ("one definition pass must use ONE config decision"). The probe's context is published back to the caller, so the snapshot still lands.
- **The tool surface is unchanged.** One wedged probe costs its own budget and nothing else: every other tool is still offered. The full `get_tool_definitions()` set is byte-identical to `main`'s.
- **A wedged probe parks one thread, not one per TTL window.** The parked probe is shared by every waiter, so the next sweep answers immediately instead of starting another thread and waiting again.
- **A build whose probes keep going silent stops probing.** Past three unanswered probes the build gives up rather than waiting once per probe.

## Tests

`tests/tools/test_check_fn_probe_timeout.py` (new). The wedged-probe cases fail on `main` with the hang itself (`a wedged check_fn must not hang its caller`), and the file also guards the two properties above plus the "a raised probe is still reported as raised" path.

```
tests/tools/test_check_fn_probe_timeout.py    9 passed
tests/tools/test_registry.py                   52 passed
tests/agent/test_builtin_memory_disabled_surface.py   13 passed
tests/hermes_cli/test_tool_availability_notices.py     4 passed
tests/agent/test_iteration_budget_warning.py           2 passed
```

`ruff` and the code-health ratchet are clean.

Fixes #131145

prs.title: fix(tools): cap execute_code kernel memory so a runaway cell dies alone
prs.body:
## What this fixes

#136403: the local `execute_code` sandbox had **no memory limit of any kind** — the only bound was a 300-second wall clock. One runaway cell allocated **180.9 GB** of virtual memory on a host with 47.7 GB RAM / 127 GB commit, which killed the Hermes backend, the Electron renderer, and unrelated host processes. The app then failed its install probe and reported "no usable Hermes install", parking an unattended run on a first-run screen for 3.5 hours.

Cap each kernel child's address space (`code_execution.memory_limit_mb`, default 4096, `0` = unlimited):

- **Windows**: a Job Object with `PROCESS_MEMORY | JOB_MEMORY | KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`, assigned right after spawn. `KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` also closes the orphan hole — a child wedged in allocation can be reached by neither `taskkill` nor the parent-death watchdog, because both need the child to be schedulable.
- **POSIX**: the runner applies `RLIMIT_AS` to itself at import from an env var, which avoids `preexec_fn` (documented as unsafe in the threaded backend that spawns kernels).

Enforcement is best-effort: if job creation or assignment fails, the kernel still spawns uncapped and the failure is logged, so a host that forbids nested job assignment does not lose `execute_code` entirely.

## Provenance — this is @ferox-fedm's fix, opened from a working account

The author wrote, tested and pushed this fix, but their account cannot create pull requests in this org (`gh pr create` → `ferox-fedm does not have the correct permissions to execute CreatePullRequest`). They asked for someone else to open it. The first commit here is **their commit, cherry-picked unchanged, with their authorship preserved** (`Ferox FEDM <gmk.one@gmail.com>`), and they are credited below. The second commit is the review follow-up.

Original branch: `ferox-fedm/hermes-agent` @ `fix/sandbox-memory-cap`, commit `d1868b6340` ("fix(tools): cap execute_code kernel memory so a runaway cell dies alone"). Thanks @ferox-fedm for the diagnosis, the Windows Job Object work and the regression test.

## Review follow-up (second commit)

- **Declare `code_execution.memory_limit_mb` in `DEFAULT_CONFIG`.** The knob was read but undeclared — undiscoverable, and unlike its siblings `kernel_idle_timeout` / `max_session_kernels`. Declaring it also obliges the docs entry (the docs-drift ratchet checks every config key).
- **Reuse the existing Windows Job Object** instead of adding a third copy of the Win32 surface: `hermes_cli/local_runtime/processes.py::_WindowsJob` already does this job and now takes an optional memory limit (`memory_capped_job()`). The duplicate class in the original commit also dropped the existing `close()` lock, so a concurrent double teardown could `CloseHandle` a recycled handle.
- **A failed POSIX `setrlimit` is no longer silent.** The original said nothing and the cell ran uncapped — the exact failure the cap exists to stop. It now writes to stderr, which the host surfaces in the cell result.
- **`@pytest.mark.platforms("windows")`** instead of a bare `skipif`, so the Windows-only job test is actually collected by the Windows OS lane (a bare `skipif` runs nowhere).
- **The config defaults moved to a sibling.** `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py` is over its line cap and may only go down, so the `code_execution` section moves to `hermes_cli/config_defaults_code_execution.py` (a pure-data leaf, the same pattern as `config_defaults_env.py`) and the new key rides along with it.

## What the fix gets right

- It caps the **actual** `execute_code` sandbox: session kernels are always on locally and there is no per-call local fallback, so `tools/code_kernel.py` is the only local spawn point.
- It covers **both** platforms the issue claims. The Windows Job Object path was verified on a native Windows host: the cell fails with `MemoryError`, the kernel survives, and the next cell on the same kernel still works. The POSIX `RLIMIT_AS` path is exercised on Linux CI by the same regression test.
- It fails **closed**: the runaway cell dies alone. The host is untouched.
- The timeout path leaks nothing: the kernel is killed and the job close mops up any descendant the tree-kill missed.
- The knob is configurable, `0` is a clean opt-out, an unparseable value falls back to the safe default (never to "uncapped").

## Tests

`tests/tools/test_code_kernel.py::TestKernelMemoryCap` — limit resolution (including the `0` opt-out and an unparseable value falling back to the safe default), Windows job attachment, and the incident's shape: a cell allocating past its budget fails while the kernel and the host survive. The regression test is bounded at 2 GiB so that a regressed cap cannot let the test itself exhaust a CI runner. Mutation-verified: with the cap disabled the same cell reports success, so the test goes red without this fix.

`tests/tools/test_code_kernel.py` — 31 passed. `tests/hermes_cli/test_local_runtime_processes.py` — 8 passed. `ruff` clean, code-health ratchet clean, docs-drift ratchet clean.

## Limits worth knowing (not changed here)

- The budget is **per kernel, not per host**: with up to 4 live kernels (plus pinned subagent kernels) a host can still reach ~16 GB of kernel address space. The 4 GiB default is a policy call a maintainer may want to tune.
- **Remote backends are not covered** (Docker / SSH / Modal): the cap is local to the local backend. This PR does not claim a global guarantee.
- The cap is read **at spawn**, so raising it needs `reset: true` or a fresh kernel.
- `memory_limit_mb: 0` removes the Windows kill-with-host containment too, not just the cap, so an orphaned kernel can outlive the backend.
- If `AssignProcessToJobObject` fails on a host that forbids nested job assignment, the child runs uncapped and logs a warning. The Desktop backend self-attaches to a kill-on-close job with `SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK`, so children break away and the assignment normally succeeds.

Fixes #136403

prs.title: fix(tui): drop stale heartbeat requeues at the delivery boundary (#135295)
prs.body:
## What this fixes

#135295: background-process heartbeat notifications reach the owning session **out of emission order**. Heartbeats are a time-ordered progress signal ("still running — here is the output since last time"), so a consumer that sees `#3` before `#1` acts on an older snapshot after already acting on a newer one. The reporter measured a live 8-heartbeat run delivering `[3, 6, 5, 7, 8, 2, 1, 4]` against an emission order of `[1..8]`.

This enforces **per-(process, session) heartbeat seq monotonicity at the delivery boundary**: a heartbeat whose seq is not newer than the last one delivered for its process session is dropped instead of re-delivered.

- Emission is untouched: single producer thread, seq assigned before `completion_queue.put()`, FIFO queue.
- The gate only touches heartbeat events that carry a `seq`; every other notification kind passes through unchanged, and no new fail-closed rejection path is added (a dropped stale beat is invisible; the next beat supersedes it).
- The UI-level dedup (which already keys heartbeats by `seq`) did not hold across independently drained sets; at the delivery boundary it now does.

## Provenance — this is @strzhao's fix, opened from a working account

The author wrote, tested and pushed this fix in #135364, then **closed it on 2026-10-18 with no comment**. The account is at exactly 5 open pull requests — the cap the repo enforces on accounts without write access (the same reason #136403's fix could not be opened by its author, and the reason kouyichi and liuhao1024 closed finished PRs too).

The first commit here is **@strzhao's commit, cherry-picked unchanged, with their authorship preserved** (`赵桂雄 <daniel21436@hotmail.com>`, which GitHub resolves to `strzhao`). Thanks @strzhao for the diagnosis, the gate and the regression test — the branch is theirs to take back.

The second commit is the follow-up below.

## Follow-up (second commit)

The regression test's fake `_run_prompt_submit` returned `None`. `_notif_submit` treats a falsy return as a **refusal** ("only the execution gate can acknowledge a claimed notification turn"), so every turn looked refused, the seq watermark never advanced, and the gate could not fire — the test failed for the wrong reason. The fake now acknowledges the turn, and the reset fixture tolerates the watermark not existing at all, so without the gate the tests fail on their own assertions instead of erroring out in the fixture.

## Why drop, not buffer-and-reorder

The issue explicitly asks whether dropping or re-ordering is the better trade. Dropping is the smaller, fail-open shape: heartbeats are interval progress signals, the *next* beat supersedes a stale one, and a reorder buffer would add queue latency plus its own reordering hazards on the same shared queue. The cost measured in the issue is a full model turn spent rendering an outdated snapshot; a dropped stale beat costs nothing. Happy to rework as a bounded reorder buffer if maintainers prefer that shape.

## Testing

`tests/tui_gateway/test_heartbeat_seq_gate.py` (new):

- **RED before the fix**: a stale beat requeued behind newer seqs is still delivered (parametrized across both drainer entry points — per-session poller and post-turn safety net); a duplicate seq is delivered twice when two independent emitted sets race. Fresh-heartbeat cross-process ordering guard is green in both states.
- **GREEN after**: 4 passed.
- **Mutations** (each reverted, revert verified by diff): gate disabled → 3 fail; watermark never advances → 3 fail; advance moved before the claim → 4 fail (self-suppression caught by the guard); per-process key made global → cross-process guard fails.

Adjacent regression: `tests/tui_gateway/test_heartbeat_wakes.py`, `tests/tui_gateway/test_launch_db_home_override_race.py`, `tests/hermes_cli/test_subagent_notification_display.py` — 16 passed. `ruff` clean, code-health ratchet clean (0 blocking, 0 advisory).

## Scope

Single concern: the TUI/Desktop delivery boundary (`tui_gateway/session_notifications.py`). The gateway-side drain (`gateway/run_notifications.py`, 2s poll + tail requeue) has the same snapshot-drain/requeue shape but different consumers (adapter-injected); it is deliberately left out — the same gate can follow there if this approach lands.

The staleness family (#120334, #120983, #127105) is complementary: those fixes re-validate **liveness**; a reordered-but-live heartbeat passes them. This gate composes with #120988's delivery-time guard rather than replacing it.

Fixes #135295

prs.title: ci(desktop): reach the Store ticket path on Windows CI (CI-2)
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Closes tracker row **CI-2** of #134889 (P0 tracker; the row was added from package 13's review of RT-21 and is not in any package).

The row says it plainly: *"The Windows Desktop attach E2E builds with `electron-builder --dir` and no `HERMES_DESKTOP_VARIANT=bundled|store`, so no agent payload is staged and the Store ticket path is never reached on Windows CI. The electron unit tests for it run only on Linux."*

Both halves are addressed:

**1. The Windows E2E now builds the bundled variant.** The packaged-build step stages the agent payload (`npm run payload`) and sets `HERMES_DESKTOP_VARIANT=bundled`, so the packaged artifact carries the runtime and the app takes the bundled launch path — the one a Store install takes — instead of bootstrapping a local install. `write-build-stamp.mjs` reads that variable to stamp the artifact kind (`bootstrap` / `bundled` / `light`) and stages the payload launchers from `agent-payload/manifest.json`, so the payload and the stamp have to travel together; before this, neither did.

**2. The Windows ticket-path electron tests now run in CI.** `js-tests.yml` had a single Ubuntu job, so the Windows-only electron tests — the native pipe tickets, the path a packaged/Store app takes — never ran anywhere. A Windows job now runs them.

The new job lists its files explicitly because the *whole* electron suite does not pass on Windows today: **24 files / 36 tests fail on a Windows host** (measured on Windows 11, Node 24). A blanket Windows leg would be red, so the list is explicit, and each file that is fixed moves out of the list and into the suite. That measurement is the useful part of this PR: it turns "the unit tests run only on Linux" from an observation into a known, bounded gap.

## Related Issue

Related: #134889 (row **CI-2**). This is not `Fixes #134889`: the tracker stays open.

- `.github/workflows/windows-desktop-attach-e2e.yml`: the packaged build stages the agent payload and builds the bundled variant (step timeout 15 → 30 min for the payload stage).

prs.title: fix(logs): skip historical output for zero-line tails
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Makes `hermes logs -n 0` skip historical entries, including with `--follow` and level filters. Currently Python's `[-0:]` slice returns all retained lines, so requesting zero history prints old entries instead.

An early return in the shared `_read_tail` path handles both the filtered and unfiltered branches. Follow mode still enters the existing follower at EOF; positive-count behavior is unchanged.

## Related Issue

No linked issue. Searched all-state issues/PRs by zero-history symptoms, `logs -n 0`, `_read_tail` and `_read_last_n_lines`. #27273 expands filtered tail search and #105437 concerns large-tail boundaries; neither fixes zero history.

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)

## Changes Made

- `hermes_cli/logs.py`: return no historical lines when zero are requested, before either filter branch.
- `tests/hermes_cli/test_logs_zero_lines.py`: one behavioral invariant across eight combinations of small/large logs, filtered/unfiltered and tail/follow. The follow-entry seam is intercepted so this regression is deterministic and does not wait for live input.

## How to Test

Using a PM-built dev/test environment (Python 3.14.9, macOS arm64), from base `adecc4024456b387b1518813b90bd60c82b51287`:

```sh
bash scripts/run_tests.sh tests/hermes_cli/test_logs_zero_lines.py tests/hermes_cli/test_logs.py --file-retries=0 -q
python scripts/check --staged
```

- New regression on unchanged production: **8 failed**, exposing unwanted historical output.
- Patched targeted run: **25 passed, 0 failed** across both complete files.
- Full canonical repository suite completed on macOS arm64 with PM Python 3.14.9, using `bash scripts/run_tests.sh -j 2 --file-retries=0 -q`. prs.title: fix(vault): sync Bitwarden on demand so items shared after bw login are fillable
prs.body:
## Summary

The Bitwarden login backend reads `bw`'s local cache, which only `bw sync` refreshes. Hermes never runs it, so a login added or shared into the vault after `bw login` (for example, into a collection the agent's account can see) never reaches `browser_vault` until the user runs `bw sync` by hand.

This PR makes the backend sync on demand: on unlock, on a stale listing, and once on a missing handle. There's no polling and no background thread.

## Changes

`agent/vault_backends/bitwarden.py`

- **Sync on unlock:** runs `bw sync` once right after a successful unlock, using the session token already held in memory.
- **Sync on listing:** `list_items()` syncs when the last successful sync is older than `vault.bitwarden.sync_on_list_seconds` (default `60`). Set it to `0` to turn on-demand sync off.
- **Sync on miss:** `get_meta()` for a handle that isn't in the cache syncs once more (debounced to 5s) and retries.
- **Non-fatal failures:** a failed sync (server offline, timeout) logs a warning and falls back to the cached items. A locked vault still raises `UnlockRequired` as before.
- **Shared sync clock:** the last-sync timestamp lives at module level, keyed by the `bw` binary path, because `enabled_backends()` builds a fresh backend object per call.

### Config

```yaml
vault:
  bitwarden:
    sync_on_list_seconds: 60   # 0 disables on-demand sync
```

## Security

`bw sync` runs through the existing `_run` path, so `BW_SESSION` goes only to that one child process. It never enters Hermes' own environment, argv, or any other child. `test_session_token_reaches_only_the_manager_call_that_uses_it` now asserts this for the sync call too.

## Tests

Six new tests in `tests/agent/test_vault_backends.py`:

- [x] Unlock syncs once and never exposes the master password
- [x] Listings sync at most once per interval
- [x] A stale clock triggers a re-sync
- [x] `sync_on_list_seconds: 0` disables sync
- [x] A missing handle triggers a re-sync and finds the newly shared item
- [x] A failed sync falls back to cached items

```bash
pytest -q tests/agent/test_vault_*.py tests/tools/test_browser_vault*.py
# 117 passed, 2 skipped
ruff check agent/vault_backends/bitwarden.py tests/agent/test_vault_backends.py tests/agent/test_vault_unlock_tokens.py
# All checks passed!
```

## Notes

- Vaultwarden and Bitwarden also offer push notifications, but the CLI doesn't expose them. A long-lived listener felt like more surface than this needs.
- No behavior change for users who never share items after `bw login`, apart from one extra `bw sync` per unlock.
