- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?**

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. It narrows where an owned session's subagent and pipeline memory operations land.
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- **If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation:** N/A. This closes a cross-principal memory isolation gap. The feature is on master only, so no release is exposed.

## Compatibility (required)

- **Backward compatible?** Yes for unowned sessions, which do not change. For owned sessions:
  - a subagent child and pipeline memory steps now use the owner's private plane
  - an owned session whose registry has `spawn_subagent` or `execute_pipeline` but was not assembled from the tool factory refuses to start
  - in an owned session, `sop_advance`, `sop_approve` and `sop_status` answer "SOP run unavailable in this session." for a run recorded with another owner or with none
- **Config / env / CLI surface changed?** No
- **Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed?** No
- **Persisted SOP runs:** a run records its owner in a new optional field. A run persisted before this change has no such field and restores as unowned, and an unowned run is still written without it.
- **Upgrade steps:** None

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <sha>`
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None
- **Runs written by this version:** an older binary ignores the owner field, so after a rollback an owned run that is still parked resumes unowned, as it does on master today.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** an owned session failing to start with `this session's tools cannot carry its owner's memory plane; refusing to pin it`.

### Notes for reviewers

- **#11225 overlap.** A trial merge with #11225's head (e38321c183) gives one conflict hunk, in `route_memory_to_principal` (`agent/agent.rs`):
  - This PR inserts the pin call just above `self.memory = Arc::clone(&routed);`.
  - #11225 deletes that line, because it assigns `self.memory` after its fallible rebind.
  - Resolution: keep the pin call and drop the line.

  Everything else merges cleanly:
  - The `zeroclaw-channels` test helper uses `AllToolsResult::from_prebuilt_tools` exactly as #11225 does.
  - The new `AllToolsResult` field and the `assemble` destructure sit away from #11225's `delegate_tool` lines.
  - `rebind_memory_tools` and `delegate.rs` are untouched.
- **Follow-up, not in this PR.** When a registry has no route, the refusal in `pin_session_memory` recognises `spawn_subagent`, `execute_pipeline`, `sop_execute`, `sop_advance` and `sop_approve` only by their wire names. A skill wrapper that exposes one of them under another name would pass the check in a hand-built registry passed to the public `assemble`, and so would `sop_status` and `sop_list`. Every production registry comes from the factory and carries a route, so this is hardening for the prebuilt-registry API. #11411's b28be2268c, with the refusal change in c52a1afc7e, covers it. It needs #11225's `builtin_target_name` and the `sop_list` route, so it lands with the SOP-read follow-up rather than here.
- **Why a route rather than the rebind.** Both tools hold a memory reach the registry rebind cannot replace: the pipeline's captured tools and the child's own construction. A shared route pinned with the session reaches both. It also reaches skill wrappers that captured them before policy filtering, which a registry-entry rebind would miss.
- **#11174.** #11174 rewrites `route_memory_to_principal` so that a refused rebind leaves the Agent unchanged. Whichever of the two lands second keeps that property with the pin as well: check that the pin can be taken, rebind, pin, then swap `self.memory`. This PR stays a draft until #11174 lands, and I'll refresh it onto that.

milestone.title: v0.9.0
milestone.description:
v0.9.0 prioritizes opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in, principal isolation, schema V4 and a CLI-only build option.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Release gates are real-provider sign-in evidence; the five principal-isolation repairs (#11234, #11220, #11225, #11230, #11266, with #11198 tracked); schema V4 (#11218); and a build-time CLI-only option that omits gateway/web assets and directs dashboard users to the standard build.

Scoped dashboard chat has a November 3 go/no-go, with sign-in alone as the fallback. November 10 is the earliest target, subject to the gates, not a committed date.

Standalone zeroclaw-gw, full gateway IPC route/parity work, cross-process webhook handling and two-process desktop packaging move to v0.9.x. Channel listeners remain in core under existing documented exceptions. These deferrals do not complete the remaining gateway roadmap.

Source of truth: #7432 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432), current release allocation. Existing implementation trackers keep their detailed work. Feature acceptance, current-head review/CI, recorded placement decisions and the v0.8.7-tag hold on breaking work remain in force.

prs.title: fix(cli): publish authorization edits from config set and config patch into the running daemon
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - `zeroclaw config set` and `zeroclaw config patch` saved `config.toml` and printed "updated" while a running daemon kept enforcing the previous authorization policy until someone reloaded it. When an edit writes or changes an authorization input (`[users]`, `[permission_profiles]`, `[oidc]`, `security.trust_daemon_uid`) and this configuration's daemon is running, the CLI now commits the edit through the daemon's own RPC config path (`config/set`, or `config/set-many` for a patch). The daemon's admitted config commit (`begin_config_commit`, then `save_and_publish_config`) already validates the policy, saves the file and publishes the new configuration and the next accepted authorization revision under the process-wide config writer lock, so the policy is in force before the CLI reports success and established connections re-resolve at their next operation. Nothing is reloaded and no connection is dropped. A `--comment` travels with the edit and the daemon writes it under the same lock, so the CLI does not touch `config.toml` after the daemon saved it.
  - The CLI only talks to the daemon that belongs to its configuration directory. That daemon counts as running while its heartbeat file beside `config.toml` is recent and names a live process. Before anything is written to the socket, the peer must be this account or root and, where the kernel reports it, the peer process must be the one the heartbeat names; otherwise the pid the daemon reports at `initialize` must match. With no confirmed daemon the CLI contacts no endpoint (an exported `ZEROCLAW_SOCKET` included), but it does probe the configuration's ownership lock: if another process holds it (a daemon still starting, before its first heartbeat, a standalone `zeroclaw gateway start`, or a `zeroclaw agent` session), the edit is saved and reported pending instead of passing silently. On Windows the CLI does not verify a named pipe's server, so it never sends an authorization edit there and reports it pending.
  - A refusal is judged by phase. When the daemon refuses the caller at the handshake (a uid outside the roster, the deny-all state), the CLI keeps its direct write and reports the edit as **pending reload**; that is the lockout-recovery path. When the daemon identifies the caller and then refuses the edit (its principal lacks the config-write grant), the command fails and nothing is saved. Pending is also reported, with the reason on stderr and as a `daemon` member in the `--json` envelope, when the daemon runs another release, fails the handshake, cannot be reached, is not this configuration's daemon, or for writes its config methods do not take (clearing a secret, creating a keyed-list row, a patch over the 256-entry batch cap). Before a pending local save, the CLI retains the effective-policy check for a daemon that shares its environment and also validates the actual persisted baseline and final TOML produced by the canonical writer, after environment masking, secret-reference restoration and dirty-path merging. Each check refuses an edit that turns its working policy into one that does not compile; an already-broken policy remains repairable in steps. Validation of the saved policy uses the writer's real merged bytes, including non-dirty file values changed since CLI staging. When the daemon rejects the edit, or is asked and never answers, the command fails and nothing is saved. A `config patch` that the daemon would apply fails before the daemon is asked if it carries any `test` op, whatever path it checks, because the `test` would be checked against the CLI's on-disk copy while every write in the patch lands on the daemon's live configuration.
  - Whether an edit is an authorization edit is decided by path (`is_auth_input_path`) or by a change in `auth_inputs`, the comparison the daemon's own publication makes, so re-asserting a value that is only on disk still reaches the daemon. The CLI owns `is_auth_input_path` privately in `src/config_publication.rs` and consumes canonical `auth_inputs` from `zeroclaw_runtime::rpc::auth`. Its guard test walks every configuration property and fails when changing a property moves `auth_inputs` without `is_auth_input_path` covering it, so adding a new authorization input cannot leave the path list behind. The CLI also owns its private heartbeat reader and freshness check, using the runtime writer's canonical state-file path and flush interval, and the daemon's refusal to overwrite a secret with a placeholder is one function (`refuses_secret_placeholder`) that both the daemon and the CLI call. Edits outside the authorization inputs never contact the daemon and their output is unchanged. `config init` never commits authorization entries through the daemon: while one runs it reports such an entry as pending, and refuses one that cannot compile until filled in (`users.<name>`, `oidc.<alias>`).
  - The authentication guide documents the full contract next to the `--json` reason codes, and no longer describes dashboard writes as reload-bound (since the supervised gateway and RPC share one authority and one live configuration, a stale statement this PR corrects deliberately); the config lifecycle and gateway API pages summarize it and link there.
- **Scope boundary:** No change to what the daemon accepts, publishes or writes, and no new RPC method. The CLI never triggers a reload. Edits outside the four authorization inputs keep their reload-bound semantics. `config migrate`, the alias helpers and the model helpers are unchanged. A standalone `zeroclaw gateway start` (like `zeroclaw agent`) holds the ownership lock without writing a heartbeat, so an authorization edit made while it runs is reported pending (`owner_unconfirmed`); it publishes its own config-API edits and picks up CLI and hand edits at its restart. `config set` still does not run the full `Config::validate()` when no daemon runs (tracked separately). The ownership lock is probed, not held: holding it from `config set` would make a daemon that starts at that moment refuse to run. The identity-checked client stays in the CLI for now; moving it into `zeroclaw_runtime::rpc::local` so `route_agent_mutation` and the shared RPC client crate can use it is #11324. Verifying a Windows named pipe's server process so Windows can publish live is #11325.
- **Blast radius:** an additive `Config::save_dirty_with_validation` callback in the existing config writer, used by pending CLI authorization saves; ordinary save methods retain their behavior. The callback receives the actual original/final documents and refuses before the atomic writer creates a backup or temporary file. It replaces the separate saved-policy preview/cache while retaining the existing effective-policy guard. Also the `config set`, `config patch` and `config init` arms in `src/main.rs` and two new modules beside it; in the runtime, the existing `auth_inputs` made public (`rpc/auth.rs`), `refuses_secret_placeholder` extracted from `stage_config_set` with identical behavior and `CONFIG_SET_MANY_MAX_ENTRIES` made `pub const` (`rpc/dispatch.rs`), and the existing heartbeat writer interval `STATUS_FLUSH_SECONDS` exposed (`daemon/mod.rs`, writer unchanged); the new heartbeat reader and auth-path classifier stay private to the CLI consumer; English Fluent keys only; three book pages. Built on #10621, which landed first: agent-targeting paths keep its routing through `route_agent_mutation`, and authorization paths, which it does not route, take this PR's. They use separate one-shot clients for now: `call_local` neither verifies which process serves the socket nor separates a refusal at the handshake from a refused request, a rejected edit and an unanswered request, and this issue needs those distinctions (#11324 tracks consolidating them).
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #10876. Closes #11323 (implements the decision recorded in this PR's review: an identified principal's refused edit fails; the save-and-pending fallback stays for refusals at the handshake). Related #11324, #11325, #11202, #10621, #11186, #10320, #10892.

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw's roster and permission profiles decide who may do what over the daemon's RPC socket. The daemon recompiles that policy whenever a config write goes through it, which is what zerocode's config editor and the web dashboard do. The command line did not: `zeroclaw config set users.alice.permission_profiles reader` rewrote the file and said "updated" while the daemon, which had never been told, kept alice's old, wider grants until someone reloaded it.

Now the command hands such an edit to the running daemon, which applies and publishes it before the command says it succeeded. If the daemon identifies the user and refuses the edit, the command fails and saves nothing. If the daemon cannot be reached, or cannot identify the user at all (the way out of a lockout), the command still saves the file as before but says plainly that the daemon is still enforcing the previous policy and that the change waits for the next reload or restart. It refuses to save an edit that would leave a working policy unable to load. Edits to anything other than the authorization sections behave exactly as they did.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, one A/B if you want to see it by hand; the same scenarios are automated in `tests/component/config_auth_publication_cli.rs`.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `cli` against a supervised daemon's local socket.
- **Setup / preconditions:** a config with `[security] trust_daemon_uid = false`, `[permission_profiles.admin] admin = true`, `[permission_profiles.reader] grants = { sessions = ["read"], config = ["read"] }`, and `[users.me] uid = <your uid>, permission_profiles = ["admin"]`; `zeroclaw daemon` running from it.
- **Steps to run:** keep a zerocode session (or a raw socket client) connected and confirm `config/set` is permitted; run `zeroclaw config set --no-interactive users.me.permission_profiles reader`; retry `config/set` on the open connection; then run `zeroclaw config set --no-interactive permission_profiles.reader.admin true`.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** stderr says the change was applied to the running daemon; the open connection's next `config/set` is refused (`-32012`), a fresh connection binds as the reader, and `config.toml` holds `["reader"]`. The reader's attempt to grant itself admin then fails with a non-zero exit and leaves `config.toml` unchanged.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** the CLI prints only "updated"; the open connection keeps admin and a fresh connection still binds as admin until `config/reload` or a restart; the second command saves `admin = true` for the next restart.

#### Current writer-boundary repair: `09981ee44fd430777b46d7892a9fa2c97981e792`

This additive follow-up preserves `1bef746eac25dab099a36227239eec9d24e26bf7`'s two-policy contract and fixes a separate merge race. The file initially contains `me.uid=1000` and `bob.uid=3000`; the CLI stages `bob.uid=2000`. While the CLI waits for the daemon handshake, another writer changes the non-dirty `me.uid` to `2000`. If the handshake refuses the unbound caller, the pending-save fallback previously checked its stale saved-policy preview and then merged the new file into duplicate `2000` uids. No environment override is needed. A mixed patch could also save its unrelated changes and report success.

The saved-policy check now runs inside the existing writer on its actual original and final TOML. The effective-policy guard is preserved, so a valid saved policy cannot excuse a collision in the CLI environment. Refusal leaves the file and dirty set unchanged and preserves the structured `validation_failed` response for the whole patch. Materialization can perform preparation before validation; the guard runs before the atomic writer's backup/temp/rename effects. ## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. The CLI connects to the daemon's owner-only local socket, which it could already reach as the same account, and presents no credential; the daemon authorizes the connection by peer credential against its accepted policy exactly as it does for zerocode, including `selector_config_write` and the recheck under the write lock.
- New external network calls? No.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? Yes. A value given to `config set` for `oidc.<alias>.client_secret` (or a secret inside a mixed `config patch`) now travels over the local socket to the daemon when the daemon commits the edit, as zerocode's config editor already sends it. It is written only after the peer uid and peer pid checks pass, never over a Windows named pipe, it is not logged, and the CLI's `--json` envelope keeps the `{path, populated}` shape for secrets.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No. Tests use the running test uid and synthetic names.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: the risk is a plaintext secret reaching an endpoint that is not this configuration's daemon. The uid check keeps it from another account's process; the pid check keeps it from another daemon of the same account (`config_set_refuses_to_publish_through_another_daemon`); with no running daemon for this configuration nothing is contacted (`config_set_ignores_another_daemon_when_this_configuration_has_none`); Windows never sends. A principal the daemon identifies cannot get around its verdict through the file: `config_set_refused_to_the_bound_principal_saves_nothing` proves a reader's attempt to grant itself admin exits non-zero, leaves `config.toml` byte-identical and leaves the live policy unchanged. Only a refusal at the handshake keeps the file write, which the same OS account could already make by hand; that is the lockout-recovery path (`config_set_refused_at_the_handshake_is_saved_and_pending`, `config_set_repairs_a_deny_all_daemon_through_the_file`), and the CLI says the edit is not in force.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? No, in four cases, all only while this configuration's daemon is running. (1) An authorization edit the daemon refuses for a principal it identified, for example a reader granting itself admin, now exits non-zero with nothing saved, where it used to save and exit 0; an edit refused at the handshake (a uid outside the roster, the deny-all state) still saves and exits 0, reported as pending with reason `refused`. (2) An authorization edit that would turn a compiling policy into one that does not (for example `config set users.bob.uid 1002` for a new entry with no `permission_profiles`, or `config init users.bob`) now fails with nothing saved instead of saving a state the next reload would turn into deny-all. (3) A `config patch` with a `test` op, on any path, fails when the daemon would apply it. (4) A `config patch` that touches the authorization sections is applied by the daemon as one batch, so its other paths also take the RPC apply boundary instead of waiting for a reload. With no daemon running, `config set`, `config patch` and `config init` are unchanged.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes: exit status as above; a stderr notice on authorization edits while a daemon runs (none with `--json`); and an optional `daemon` member in the `--json` envelopes of `config set`, `config patch` and `config init`: `{"applied": true}` or `{"applied": false, "pending_reload": true, "reason": ...}` with the reasons `refused`, `version_mismatch`, `handshake`, `unreachable`, `other_daemon`, `unverified_endpoint`, `owner_unconfirmed`, `not_replayable`, `offline_command` (documented in the authentication guide). Existing members are unchanged.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No.
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: none. Scripts that create a roster or OIDC entry field by field with `config set` or `config init` while the daemon runs should send the fields in one `config patch`; scripts that relied on a refused CLI edit still landing at the next restart should make the edit as an account with the config-write grant.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** after landing, revert the landed PR commit and reconcile dependent work. Reverting only `09981ee44fd430777b46d7892a9fa2c97981e792` restores the preceding saved-policy preview and its demonstrated dirty-merge race while retaining the earlier effective-policy behavior. No schema/data migration is introduced by this repair.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** an authorization `config set` that reports `pending_reload` with reason `other_daemon`, `owner_unconfirmed` or `unreachable` while the daemon is healthy; a `config set` that waits up to about 38 s on a stuck daemon before failing with an unknown outcome; `RPC authorization denied` audit lines on the daemon for a CLI caller. `grep 'did not answer an authorization edit'` in the CLI's trace output catches the unknown-outcome case.

milestone.description:

prs.title: feat(rpc): SOP parity for cancel, dispatch-event, decision-models and graph-legend
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** As part of the v0.9.0 gateway split, this PR adds the RPC methods the gateway will call once it moves out of process. The daemon RPC surface gains the SOP operations it was missing next to the gateway's HTTP routes. `sops/decide` also stops treating a client-supplied label as the approver's identity.
  - **`sops/decide` by run id, with the real principal.** `name` is now optional; the run id selects the run, and a `name` that is given must be the run's SOP. The approver the group-approval policy sees now comes from the connection's authentication. It used to be `ApprovalPrincipal::cli(tui_id)`, and the TUI id is client-supplied (accepted unsigned when TUI signing is off) and "grants no authority" by the dispatcher's own rule. That meant a claimed TUI id could satisfy a bare or `cli:` group member. The new mapping:
    - **Native pairing bearer:** the paired-token subject, exactly what the gateway's HTTP and WebSocket routes derive from the same token. `http:<subject>` members match, and one token is one quorum voter on every surface. The ledger's channel records `rpc`.
    - **Any other authenticated principal** (a `[users]` entry, an OIDC subject): a new `principal` approval source keyed on the canonical principal id, so members name it `principal:<id>` or bare.
    - **The unauthenticated shared operator:** anonymous, like `zeroclaw sop approve`. It cannot satisfy a `required_group`.
    - The approver's entitlement to the run's agents, checked before the decision reaches the broker, is checked again on freshly resolved grants under the lock that resolves the decision.
  - **`sops/cancel`** `{run_id, name?, reason?}`: the gateway's safe cancel (the step in flight finishes, and the run stops at the next boundary). It's idempotent (`outcome`: `requested`, `already_requested`, `cancelled` or `already_terminal`) and attributes the cancellation to the same principal. A scoped principal must be entitled to the run's agents, and that is checked again on freshly resolved grants once the lock that cancels is held, so a grant or agent entitlement withdrawn while the request waited for the engine cannot cancel. A run whose procedure is no longer loaded is refused for a scoped principal rather than passed.
  - **`sops/dispatch-event`** `{path, payload?}`: the webhook fan-in behind `POST /sop/{*rest}`. The caller keeps authenticating the delivery and applying idempotency, as the HTTP route does today. A scoped principal must be entitled to every matched procedure's agents, and that is checked where the run starts, not only when the call arrives. A preflight refuses early, matching on the topic as dispatch normalizes it, so a path that differs from a trigger only in characters the normalization removes (a zero-width space, say) cannot match nothing at the preflight and a forbidden procedure at dispatch. The enforcing check runs at run admission: after any decision-model wait, on the normalized match set, under the engine lock that starts the run, against freshly re-resolved grants. A grant or agent entitlement withdrawn while a decision model deliberates starts nothing, and a call whose every match is refused there returns `FORBIDDEN`. Each run that starts on an agent step is handed to a headless driver that holds the daemon's live configuration and reads it at each step's execution boundary: after the decision wait, the driver lease, generation admission and every engine lock the step takes, with nothing that waits between that read and the owner check, the tool policy and the turn. An agent disabled or re-profiled at any point before a step runs is not run under its former settings. The fan-in core (driver admission and result shaping) moves into `zeroclaw-runtime` as `sop::dispatch_webhook_event`, and the gateway route now calls it, so the two surfaces cannot drift.
  - **`sops/decision-models`** and **`sops/graph-legend`**: the two read-only authoring lookups. Decision models come from a shared `sop::decision_model_options`, also used by the gateway route (it never lists an API key).
- **Scope boundary:** The `sops/subscribe-runs` stream belongs to separate work on the subscription hub, so there are no run-change notifications or `seq` here. There's no new service principal and no change to who may call these methods beyond the existing `sops` grant classification. The gateway's own `decide` and `cancel` routes keep their current identity derivation. Idempotency for webhook deliveries stays in the gateway; moving it is outside this PR.
- **Blast radius:**
  - `zeroclaw-runtime`: `Method` gains four variants (compile-forced `authz` arms). The SOP approval principal gains a `Principal` source and three RPC constructors. The ledger's vote replay learns the `principal` label. There's a new `sop::surface` module. `sop::dispatch_webhook_event` takes the live configuration handle rather than a `Config`. The headless driver entry points accept a `SopDriverConfig`: `Snapshot`, built from a `Config` as every other caller still passes, or `Live`, which the driver reads once per step at the step's execution boundary. The RPC agent selector and SOP agent checks gain grant-parametric forms, so admission and the rechecks run one predicate. `SopIngress` gains an optional run-admission check (`with_admission_check`), and `ContentSafety::normalize_topic` and `sop::dispatch::untrusted_topic_matches` expose the topic normalization dispatch already applied, so an authorization preflight matches the same form.
  - `zeroclaw-api`: `SopDecideRequest.name` becomes `Option<String>` (wire-compatible; no in-tree struct literals). There are new `SopCancelRequest` and `SopDispatchEventRequest` types.
  - `zeroclaw-gateway`: the `/sop/*` webhook handler and the decision-models route call the shared runtime helpers, with no response change. The webhook handler passes its live configuration handle, so its drivers read the configuration when each step runs.
  - Docs: the approval-identity section of `sop/syntax.md`.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11001 (matching gateway behavior over RPC), Related #11000, Related #8289.
- **Labels:** `docs`, `gateway`, `runtime`, `size:XL` (labeler-applied; `risk:*` is left for a maintainer).

### What this does, simply

The gateway is going to become a separate process that talks to the daemon over its RPC socket, so every SOP action the dashboard can take has to exist as an RPC method first. Four were missing: cancelling a run, delivering a webhook event, listing decision models, and fetching the graph legend. This PR adds them.

It also closes a trust gap in approving an SOP checkpoint over RPC. The daemon recorded the approver as whatever TUI id the client presented, and approval groups could match on that label, so a client could claim to be someone on the approver list. Now the approver is whoever the connection actually authenticated as: the same paired device the web dashboard would see, or the signed-in user. A connection that never authenticated can't satisfy a policy that requires a group.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes. The identity change is observable with one paired token and a policy-gated checkpoint.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `tui` (daemon RPC).
- **Setup / preconditions:** an SOP whose first step is a checkpoint with `policy: prod`; `[sop.approval.policies.prod] required_group = "release"`; `[sop.approval.groups.release] members = ["http:<sha256 of your paired token>"]`; and `gateway.paired_tokens` containing that token.
- **Steps to run:**
  1. Start a run of the SOP (it parks at the checkpoint).
  2. Over the RPC socket, `initialize` with `auth_token` = the paired token, then `sops/decide {"run_id": "<id>", "decision": "approve"}` with no `name`.
  3. Repeat step 2 from a connection that is not paired, presenting `tui_id` = `ZeroClawOperator`, with `"ZeroClawOperator"` added to the group.
  4. `sops/cancel {"run_id": "<id of a second parked run>"}`, twice.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** step 2 resumes the run. Step 3 is refused with `-32010` and the run stays parked. Step 4 reports `outcome: "cancelled"` and then `outcome: "already_terminal"`.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** step 2 is refused (`name` is required, and the approver is `cli:<tui id>`, which is not in the group). Step 3 clears the gate on a claimed label. `sops/cancel` does not exist.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `CI Required Gate` on the head. Test covers the runtime `rpc::`/`sop::` suites and the gateway suite, including the existing `/sop/*` webhook route tests that now run through the shared helper.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** none for the changed surface. No zerocode change, because zerocode already sends `name`, which is still accepted.
- **Commands run and tail output (local, Rust 1.96.1, at e69451ead6 on master 4f93bf5399):**

```
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
(clean)
$ bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh
Comment hygiene gate passed.
$ cargo check -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-gateway -p zeroclaw-api --all-targets
Finished `dev` profile (clean)
$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-gateway --all-targets
(no findings in the files this PR changes)
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- sop rpc:: security::external_content
test result: ok. 1485 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored
(one earlier run of this suite timed out in session_prompt_waits_for_queued_provider_update_transaction,
a session test this PR does not touch; it passed alone five times and in the full rerun above)
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-gateway -p zeroclaw-api
test result: ok. 277 passed; 0 failed
test result: ok. 621 passed; 0 failed
test result: ok. 5 passed; 0 failed; 7 ignored
test result: ok. 9 passed; 0 failed
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed
```

  New tests: sops_decide_sees_the_paired_subject_the_gateway_sees, sops_decide_counts_one_paired_credential_as_one_voter, sops_decide_sees_the_authenticated_roster_principal, sops_decide_ignores_a_claimed_tui_id, sops_decide_checks_a_named_sop_against_the_run, sops_cancel_is_idempotent_by_run_id, sops_dispatch_event_starts_webhook_sops, sops_dispatch_event_authorizes_the_normalized_topic, the five sop_run_start_* admission tests, the seven sop_driver_* configuration tests, the three sops_cancel_*_while_waiting_for_the_engine_* tests, the two sops_decide_*_while_waiting_for_the_engine_* tests, sops_decision_models_and_graph_legend_serve_the_gateway_shapes, sops_parity_methods_are_classified, principal::rpc_paired_subject_is_the_same_voter_as_the_gateway, principal::rpc_principals_are_keyed_by_their_canonical_id, surface::decision_models_are_sorted_and_carry_no_key, and dispatch::untrusted_topic_matches_uses_the_normalized_topic.

  With the fixes reverted, the tests that guard them fail and their controls pass. Without the admission check and with a raw-topic preflight, the revoked, narrowed and reowned admission tests, the normalized-topic test and the helper test fail. Without the cancel and decide rechecks and with the driver configuration read before dispatch, the revoked and narrowed cancel tests, the revoked decide test, and the disabled-owner and changed-policy driver tests fail, while the unchanged cancel, decide and driver controls pass. The driver's configuration read is pinned to the step boundary: handing the driver a copy when the dispatch returns fails the step-boundary and admission-wait tests, and reading the configuration once when the driver starts fails the step-boundary tests; the decision-wait tests and every control pass under both.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Pinned by tests:
  - A paired device in the group clears a checkpoint by run id alone, and a paired device outside it is refused, with the run left parked.
  - One paired token voting twice does not meet a quorum of two, and a second member's token does.
  - A roster user named as `principal:<id>` clears the gate, and another roster user does not.
  - A claimed TUI id matching both a bare and a `cli:` member is refused.
  - A named SOP that is not the run's is refused.
  - Cancel is idempotent and refuses an unknown run or the wrong SOP.
  - A webhook path starts its SOP; an unmatched path reports `no_match`; an empty path is refused.
  - A dispatch parked at its decision model starts no run when, during the wait, the caller loses `sops:execute`, its agent entitlement is narrowed away from the procedure's agent, or the procedure is redefined to a forbidden agent. The same wait with the policy unchanged or widened starts the run, so re-resolution is proven, not a blanket refusal.
  - A webhook path carrying a zero-width character that normalizes to another agent's trigger is refused, and no run starts.
  - The procedure's agent disabled in the live configuration while the dispatch is parked at its decision model, while the dispatch waits to admit its driver into the generation, or while the driver is parked at the step's execution boundary (after every wait it makes): the run starts, but the driver refuses the disabled agent and no turn runs. A risk profile replaced at the decision or at the step boundary is the one the step policy is built from, and an unchanged configuration runs as the configured owner.
  - A `sops/cancel` waiting on the engine lock while the caller's `sops:execute` grant is withdrawn, or its agent selector narrowed away from the run's agent, is refused and leaves the run, its cancellation record and its claim untouched; with nothing changed it cancels.
  - A `sops/decide` approval waiting on the engine lock while the caller's `sops:execute` grant is withdrawn is refused and the run stays parked; with nothing changed it resumes the run.
  - Decision models never list an API key, and the graph legend serves the canonical legend through the full request path.

  NOT verified: an OIDC-authenticated principal end to end (it takes the same `rpc_principal` branch as the roster user, keyed on `Principal.id`), and a live daemon. The tests use the in-process dispatcher.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A. No rendered interface changed.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** workspace check and clippy, and the full workspace test suite. CI runs them; the changed crates were checked with `--all-targets` and their suites run locally.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. The four methods use the existing `sops` grant classification: `read` for the two lookups, `execute` for cancel and dispatch-event, matching `sops/run` and `sops/decide`. Scoped principals are held to the agent selector of every procedure they act on.
- New external network calls? No.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? Yes, narrowing. The approval identity on RPC now comes from the authenticated connection. A native bearer contributes only its SHA-256 subject, which the connection already retained for revocation checks; the bearer itself is never stored. A client-claimed TUI id no longer reaches the approval broker.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No. `sops/dispatch-event` payloads enter the same untrusted fan-in path the HTTP webhook route already uses.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: covered above.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Wire: yes. `name` stays accepted on `sops/decide`, and the new methods are additive. Behavior: a `sops/cancel` or `sops/decide` whose caller lost the needed authority while it waited for the SOP engine is refused. A `sops/dispatch-event` call accepted into decision evaluation can now be refused with `FORBIDDEN` if the caller's authority over the matched procedure is gone by the time the run would be admitted. An approval-group member that matched only a TUI id (a bare label or `cli:<tui id>`) no longer matches over RPC. That match was never an authenticated identity, and the docs already said the CLI path is anonymous. Operators name the paired-token subject (`http:<subject>`) or the principal (`principal:<id>`) instead. Rust source: `SopDecideRequest.name` is now `Option<String>`.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: replace any approval-group member that named a TUI id with the approver's paired-token subject or `principal:<id>`, as described in the updated `sop/syntax.md`.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert` of this PR's squash commit. Votes recorded with the new `principal` source are not recognised by an older binary's quorum replay, so after a rollback they stop counting toward a pending quorum (fail closed, the gate stays waiting). Re-approve from a surface the older binary recognises.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** a policy-gated `sops/decide` over RPC refused with `-32010` for an approver who should qualify. Check that the group names `http:<subject>` for a paired device or `principal:<id>` for a signed-in user, and that the connection authenticated as that identity (`initialize` reports `principal_id`). A `/sop/*` webhook response differing from before would indicate the shared helper diverged.

prs.title: feat(install): install the CLI-only build and switch it to the standard build only on request
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** the CLI-only build (`cargo generate features --selection cli-only`, built and tested in CI since #11976) had no supported way to be installed, and `zeroclaw update` would have replaced it with the standard build and its dashboard without asking.
  - **The installer.** `install.sh --cli-only` (or `--preset cli-only`) builds from source with the registry's `cli-only` feature list for the host target.
    - If the list can't be resolved, it stops. Falling back to Cargo's defaults would install the dashboard build.
    - The CLI-only set is complete, so right after parsing, before it installs anything, the installer refuses every option that would change it: `--features` (and `ZEROCLAW_CARGO_FEATURES`), `--full` or another preset, `--with-gateway` and `--minimal`. It refuses `--features` outright, because it cannot see Cargo's feature graph: `--features default` alone would turn the gateway back on.
    - It skips the dashboard build and offers only the CLI quickstart.
  - **The updater.** `zeroclaw update` picked the standard archive in every build. Releases publish only the standard build, so a CLI-only build now switches to it only on request:
    - Without a flag, `zeroclaw update` installs nothing and explains the choice. The standard build adds the dashboard and web gateway, which start with the daemon, by default on `127.0.0.1:42617` with pairing required. `zeroclaw update --standard` switches; re-running `install.sh --cli-only` keeps the CLI-only build. On a newer release the explanation is the error (exit 1); on the same or an older release it follows "Already up to date" (exit 0).
    - With `--standard`, it prints one line saying it is switching, then installs the standard archive through the same download, `SHA256SUMS` check, backup, swap and smoke test as a standard build. It switches on the release's own version too, because the build changes; a downgrade still needs `--force`.
    - `--version` and `--force` combine with `--standard`. `--check` and its `--json` output are unchanged. A standard build accepts the flag and ignores it.
  - **Docs.** The Linux setup page gets a CLI-only section, which says how to install it, how to update it and stay CLI-only, and how to switch to the standard build. The remote zerocode page notes that a CLI-only daemon has no gateway pairing, so remote clients use OIDC or run zerocode on the server over SSH.
  - **Strings.** The refusal and the switching line are new English Fluent keys (`cli-update-cli-only-needs-standard`, `cli-update-switching-to-standard`), and the English `update` help mentions `--standard`. Other locales show the English text until their catalogs are filled.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - No release workflow change. Releases keep one standard archive per target, with the dashboard and web gateway, and the CLI-only build is a source build through `install.sh --cli-only`.
  - No change to how standard builds install or update.
- **Blast radius:** `src/commands/update.rs`, the `update` flags in `src/main.rs`, the English CLI catalog (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/locales/en/cli.ftl`), `install.sh` and its renderer (`xtask/src/generate/install_sh.rs`), and two docs pages.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11971. Related #7432.
  - #11269, #11973, #11974, #11975 and #11976 delivered the rest of #11971: the feature edges, the agent cascade, the gated tests, the standard-build pointers in `gateway`, `desktop`, `status` and `self-test`, and the CLI-only CI lane with its artifact ratchet.
  - This PR adds the remaining two acceptance criteria: `install.sh --cli-only` with the documented selection, and a `zeroclaw update` that never replaces a CLI-only build unless asked to with `--standard`.

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw can be built without the web dashboard, for servers that only run agents and channels. Until now you had to work out the build flags yourself. With this change, one installer flag, `--cli-only`, builds and installs it.

It also stops `zeroclaw update` from quietly replacing that build with the normal one, dashboard included. Releases only ship the normal build, so `zeroclaw update` now asks you to choose: run the installer again to stay CLI-only, or run `zeroclaw update --standard` to switch to the normal build.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, for the installer, and for `update` if you have a CLI-only build.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `cli` (`install.sh`, `zeroclaw update`)
- **Setup / preconditions:** a checkout of this branch with Rust installed. For `update`, a CLI-only build of this branch and network access to GitHub releases.
- **Steps to run:**
  - `sh install.sh --cli-only --dry-run --skip-quickstart --no-modify-path`
  - in a CLI-only build: `zeroclaw update`, then `zeroclaw update --standard`
- **Expected on this branch (after):**
  - the installer prints `[dry-run] Would run: cargo install --path . --locked --force --no-default-features --features <the cli-only list>`, and no dashboard build;
  - `sh install.sh --cli-only --features gateway --dry-run` stops with `✗ --cli-only is a complete feature set and takes no --features (or ZEROCLAW_CARGO_FEATURES); …`;
  - `zeroclaw update` changes nothing and prints the explanation shown under "`zeroclaw update` through the command" below: as the error on a newer release, after "Already up to date" otherwise;
  - `zeroclaw update --standard` prints the switching line and installs the standard build, also when the release has the same version.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** the installer stops with `✗ Unknown option: --cli-only. Run: install.sh --help`; `--preset cli-only` stops with `✗ Unknown preset 'cli-only'. Expected: minimal or full`. `zeroclaw update` in a build without the gateway installs the standard build without asking.

### How I tested

Tested on Linux x86_64 at e6e4b0486d (tree `23b6f52e09`), which changes only `src/commands/update.rs` from the previous head dc597de56e. `$LIST` is the resolved CLI-only set (`cargo generate features --selection cli-only --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, 27 features). Every test binary, installer run and `zeroclaw` binary ran in a network namespace with loopback only. `$UPDATE` is the filter `test(/^commands::update::/) | test(update_cli_parses_standard_with_version_and_force)`: the updater tests plus the parse test for `--standard`.

The head is now cdc0172d16 (tree `d7ed45f2e7`), a merge of master f87368a6aa into e6e4b0486d. It brings in #12129 (Wasmtime 48.0.8, which fixes the RUSTSEC-2026-0420 to 0424 advisories the `Security` check reported) and the six master commits before it. None of them changes a file this PR changes, so the PR's diff is the same as at e6e4b0486d. The gates ran again on the merge:

```text
# On the merge cdc0172d16
cargo fmt --all -- --check                                                 → exit 0
cargo metadata --locked; cargo verify-project && cargo fetch --locked      → exit 0
cargo audit (0.22.2)                                                       → exit 0, 1395 advisories loaded; none of RUSTSEC-2026-0420 to 0424
cargo deny check                                                           → advisories ok, bans ok, licenses ok, sources ok
cargo check --locked --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop --no-default-features   → exit 0, no warnings
cargo check --locked --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop --all-targets           → exit 0, no warnings
cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw --all-targets -- -D warnings             → exit 0
cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw --all-targets --no-default-features --features "$LIST" -- -D warnings → exit 0
cargo clippy --locked --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop --all-targets --features ci-all -- -D warnings → exit 0
cargo nextest run --locked -p zeroclaw --no-default-features --features "$LIST" --lib --bins -E "$UPDATE" → 131 passed, 0 failed
cargo nextest run --locked -p zeroclaw --lib --bins -E "$UPDATE"           → 125 passed, 0 failed

A same-version switch installs; `install.sh --cli-only` refuses every option that would change its feature set.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** a fresh real install and an update from GitHub itself, because both need the network (and no release has this code). The full workspace `cargo nextest run` was also skipped, because `Test` runs it.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No, unless the user asks. With `--standard`, a CLI-only build becomes the standard build, whose daemon starts the web gateway (by default on `127.0.0.1:42617`, pairing required), as in any standard install. The refusal says this before the user opts in.
- New external network calls? No. The updater fetches the same release metadata. With `--standard`, a CLI-only build downloads the standard archive and checks it against `SHA256SUMS`, as a standard build does.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A. Without the flag the updater fails closed: a CLI-only build refuses rather than install a different build.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes. Standard builds install and update exactly as before; `--standard` is accepted and has no effect there.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes:
  - new `install.sh` flags `--cli-only` and `--preset cli-only`;
  - new `zeroclaw update --standard`;
  - in a build without the gateway, `zeroclaw update` without `--standard` now installs nothing and explains why: it refuses a newer release (exit 1) and adds the explanation after "Already up to date" otherwise (exit 0). Before, it would have installed the standard build.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: none for standard builds. CLI-only builds update by re-running `install.sh --cli-only`, or switch with `zeroclaw update --standard`.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <sha>`.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None.
- **Observable failure symptoms:**
  - `install.sh --cli-only` stopping with "Could not resolve the CLI-only feature set", or refusing an option that does not change the feature set;
  - `zeroclaw update --standard` in a CLI-only build, or `zeroclaw update` in a standard build, reporting "no suitable binary found for this platform" when a release has its archive. The updater tests in both builds guard these cases.

milestone.title: v0.9.0
milestone.description:
v0.9.0 prioritizes opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in, principal isolation, schema V4 and a CLI-only build option.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Release gates are real-provider sign-in evidence; the five principal-isolation repairs (#11234, #11220, #11225, #11230, #11266, with #11198 tracked); schema V4 (#11218); and a build-time CLI-only option that omits gateway/web assets and directs dashboard users to the standard build.

Scoped dashboard chat has a November 3 go/no-go, with sign-in alone as the fallback. November 10 is the earliest target, subject to the gates, not a committed date.

Standalone zeroclaw-gw, full gateway IPC route/parity work, cross-process webhook handling and two-process desktop packaging move to v0.9.x. Channel listeners remain in core under existing documented exceptions. These deferrals do not complete the remaining gateway roadmap.

Source of truth: #7432 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432), current release allocation. Existing implementation trackers keep their detailed work. Feature acceptance, current-head review/CI, recorded placement decisions and the v0.8.7-tag hold on breaking work remain in force.

  • Android: Make prop_info an extern type (#5561)
  • Apple: Mach API is now available on non-MacOS targets again. This should resolve some issues building ecosystem crates. (#5612), (#5636)
  • FreeBSD: Add back NOTE_PCTRLMASK with a deprecation warning (#5600)

0.2.190

There is now a single config for enabling 64-bit time_t: libc_unstable_time64. This can be set unconditionally; it opts in to 64-bit time_t on the following platforms that use 32-bit by default:

  • 32-bit Linux-GNU
  • 32-bit Linux-uClibc
  • 32-bit Linux-musl. Note that setting this flag also enables some other changes that happend in musl v1.2.
  • 32-bit Windows-GNU
  • ESP-IDF (all targets with this environment are 32-bit)

Most other 32-bit platforms are either already using 64-bit time_t, or are considered legacy and will not be gaining support from their upstream maintainers.

You can enable this using RUSTFLAGS:

RUSTFLAGS='--cfg=libc_unstable_time64' cargo ...

Note that there may still be some changes to features gated by this config option, hence "unstable"

  • FreeBSD: Add back NOTE_PCTRLMASK with a deprecation warning (#5600)

0.2.190

There is now a single config for enabling 64-bit time_t: libc_unstable_time64. This can be set unconditionally; it opts in to 64-bit time_t on the following platforms that use 32-bit by default:

  • 32-bit Linux-GNU
  • 32-bit Linux-uClibc
  • 32-bit Linux-musl. Note that setting this flag also enables some other changes that happend in musl v1.2.
  • 32-bit Windows-GNU
  • ESP-IDF (all targets with this environment are 32-bit)

Most other 32-bit platforms are either already using 64-bit time_t, or are considered legacy and will not be gaining support from their upstream maintainers.

You can enable this using RUSTFLAGS:

RUSTFLAGS='--cfg=libc_unstable_time64' cargo ...

Note that there may still be some changes to features gated by this config option, hence "unstable"

prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - `send_message_to_peer`'s in-process delivery path starts the recipient turn in a detached `zeroclaw_spawn::spawn!` task.
  - Task-locals (including the active headless SOP step scope) do not cross that spawn, so the recipient rebuilt its full tool surface and escaped the step's capability boundary.
  - Capture `active_headless_step_scope()` before spawn and restore it with `with_inherited_headless_step_scope`, matching `delegate` and `spawn_subagent`.
- **Scope boundary:** Does not change Act/autonomy checks on the sender, external-peer delivery, or live (non-headless) SOP step scope publishing.
- **Blast radius:** Recipient turns started from a scoped headless step now see the step's tool exclusions; unscoped / non-headless peer sends are unchanged (`None` inherits as a no-op).
- **Linked issue(s):** Fixes #12169

### What this does, simply

When a headless SOP step is only allowed to message a peer, calling `send_message_to_peer` must not give the peer agent the whole tool list. The step's limit was kept in a task-local; the peer turn runs in a new task that never saw that limit. This PR copies the limit into the peer turn the same way `delegate` and `spawn_subagent` already do for the work they start.

prs.title: fix(tools): enforce Act policy on send_message_to_peer
prs.body:
## Summary
`send_message_to_peer` could start another agent's turn (or post to an external peer) without consulting the sender's autonomy level or action budget. Sibling Act tools (`a2a_send`, `spawn_subagent`, `delegate`) already call `enforce_tool_operation(ToolOperation::Act, …)` at the start of `execute`.

This PR threads a `SecurityPolicy` into `SendMessageToPeerTool` (registration passes the turn's policy; convenience constructors derive via `SecurityPolicy::for_agent`) and refuses Act before any delivery path runs.

Fixes #12167

## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`.
- **What changed and why:** Propose a bounded runtime-placement exception for #12130's configurable daemon RPC session quotas. The existing orphan-retirement exception explicitly excludes changing the session cap. Name the existing owners, exact paths, intended extraction destination and review conditions before the feature is implemented.
- **Scope boundary:** One proposed exception row. No runtime, configuration, protocol, authentication, session-lifecycle or quota implementation changes. The approval field remains pending and must receive the actual Core approval link and date before merge.
- **Blast radius:** Future quota implementation within existing runtime owners. The record does not permit a new subsystem or extend exceptions to unrelated work.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #12130. Related #8289, #11964 and #11986.

### What this does, simply

The quota feature will prevent concurrent session creation from consuming all daemon capacity, while reserving space for authorized local operators. That capacity belongs to the existing SessionStore, which still lives in the transitional runtime crate. Its current exception only allows orphan cleanup and expressly excludes changing the 64-session cap.

This PR requests permission to implement that bounded feature where its state already lives. Extracting the complete RPC/session and Agent-construction lifecycle first would turn the quota change into a much larger ownership refactor. Configuration and transcripts keep their current owners, and the row points runtime work toward the planned zeroclaw-kernel extraction.

This is the separate placement decision required by [ADR-016](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/1c1cd118ac536a1dd1bc79b9cce69cbdc04e4f29/docs/book/src/architecture/decisions/ADR-016-holding-crate-exceptions.md#L54). prs.title: docs(runtime): propose bounded RPC denial reason exception
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** Adds one row to the active-exception table in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/AGENTS.md`, proposing a bounded holding-crate exception for the stable RPC denial reasons and reason-keyed denial records in #11289 (which closes #11005). The crate guide requires the exception to be recorded before the feature merges, and a feature pull request cannot grant itself one, so the row is proposed here on its own. It answers the open review item on #11289 (`src/rpc/auth.rs:97`, 2026-10-12), which found that no recorded exception covers RPC denial reporting.
- **Scope boundary:** Documentation only. The permission covers exactly what #11289 changes in `zeroclaw-runtime` at `5740f15a35` (three files: `src/rpc/auth.rs`, `src/rpc/dispatch.rs` and `locales/en/cli.ftl`): the `RpcDenialReason` identifier type with `as_str`, its private `code` and `message_key` mappings and `From<DenyReason>`; on the existing `AuthDenied`, the private `reason` field and `reason()` accessor, the private `new`, `with_message` and `with_values` builders, the `quoted` helper, the 21 named `pub(crate)` constructors that replace `auth_required` and `forbidden` (with `from_deny_reason` rebuilt on the private `with_message` and the five other `auth.rs` functions named in the row building their denials through them), and `audit_attrs`, which gives the existing `RPC authorization denied` record its `method`, `reason`, `denial_message`, `code`, `principal_id` and `auth_provider` attributes; in `src/rpc/dispatch.rs`, `audit_denial` emitting those attributes, `RpcDispatcher::refuse`, the `authorize` gate and the 21 other refusal functions named in the row building their denials through the constructors or refusing through `refuse`, the gate attributing a denial after a failed revalidation to the principal whose binding it drops, the `steering_admission` closure's record changes (its ownership and remote local-capability refusals recorded under their own reasons, the latter with that reason's `-32003` on the record while the steer is still answered `-32012`; the refusals its binding checks record themselves recorded once rather than twice, so a steer refused because its agent's policy cannot be resolved leaves no denial record), the selectors' refusals of an uninitialized connection now recorded, the retired `GLOBAL_STREAM_SCOPED_DENIAL` literal, the fourteen `rpc-auth-*` keys and their translator comment (thirteen replacing an inline literal, `rpc-auth-session-local-capabilities` feeding only the record), and focused tests. `RpcDenialReason`, `as_str` and `reason()` are `pub`; no other crate consumes them. `DenyReason`, the JSON-RPC error codes and the grants stay in `zeroclaw-api`, and the record sink in `zeroclaw-log`, so they need no runtime permission; the root `AGENTS.md` bullet and the `docs/book` section that #11289 adds are outside the holding crate. It excludes any identifier in a client response, recording a refused `initialize` handshake or the other refusals answered without an `AuthDenied`, and any new RPC method, grant source, config key, record kind, record sink, retained runtime state or non-English locale.
- **Blast radius:** Contributor placement guidance only. No runtime behavior changes. The row is not active until a Core Team member other than the author approves it; the `Approved by` cell is filled with that review's permalink before merge, so merging this pull request is what records the vote.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11005 and #11289 (head `5740f15a35`). #11289 lands after #11326, whose global-stream wording the row's key note reflects. Precedent: #11701, #12058, #11963, and the #11286 row already in the table, which covers `src/rpc/auth.rs` and `locales/en/cli.ftl` but is limited to roster-bound pairing tokens.

### What this does, simply

`zeroclaw-runtime` is a holding crate: new code there is supposed to move to its own crate, and the Core Team records each deliberate exception in a table so the extraction debt stays visible. #11289 gives every RPC authorization refusal built through `AuthDenied` a stable identifier such as `grant_missing` or `agent_not_entitled`, writes that identifier into the denial record the daemon already emits (the refusal text moves to its own `denial_message` attribute), moves the refusals' inline English literals into the Fluent catalogue (the gate's grant refusal and the global-stream, SOP, session-environment and upload-ownership refusals as well as the selectors'), and keeps the principal and provider on the record when a policy change drops a connection's binding. Clients receive the same codes and English text as before (the global-stream refusal takes the wording #11326 gives it), and never the identifier. The set of recorded refusals changes slightly: the selectors' refusals of a connection that never initialized are now recorded, a steer refused by its agent, workspace or environment check is recorded once rather than twice, and a steer refused because its agent's policy cannot be resolved is no longer recorded. This row asks permission for exactly those changes, with the RPC authorization-gate and inbound-authentication owners in the planned kernel extraction as their destination.

Why placement is right: every one of these additions changes code the crate already holds. On master, `AuthDenied`, with its `auth_required`, `forbidden` and `from_deny_reason` constructors, sits in `src/rpc/auth.rs` next to `RpcInboundAuth`, `AcceptedAuthState` and `AuthorityLease`; `RpcDispatcher::authorize`, `audit_denial` (which already writes the `RPC authorization denied` record, with the message as its `reason`), `current_authority`, the selectors and `still_authorized` sit in `src/rpc/dispatch.rs`; and the handshake denials already resolve `rpc-auth-*` keys in `locales/en/cli.ftl`. The reason is set by the code that decides to refuse, so it lives where that decision is made, and it reaches only the log record: `rpc_err(denied.code, denied.message)` still sends the client the code and text alone, so the identifier is not part of the wire contract `zeroclaw-api` owns, and `zeroclaw-log` records whatever attributes the gate hands it. Moving the vocabulary out on its own would split the gate from its refusals ahead of the kernel extraction that owns the RPC boundary, which is the case the exception policy describes. #11005 names `src/rpc/{auth,dispatch}.rs` and the catalogue among the work's likely files.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A`; documentation-only change to a Markdown table. Please review the row's scope against the #11289 head (`5740f15a35`): `git diff --stat 5d4b18d335 5740f15a35 -- crates/zeroclaw-runtime` lists the three files it names.

### How I tested

#### Current integration: `3e50a4720b1f959d0346390030d0319c347fab27`

This additive merge brings in master `f87368a6aa53d16b0bd7411b002331a22622c2a7`, including the merged Wasmtime security repair #12129. The complete runtime instruction file remains byte-identical to this PR's preceding head; the owned diff is still the same one-row addition. Approval status and scope are unchanged. Both dependency files exactly match master.

On this exact revision, the docs quality gate and docs links gate passed with `DOCS_FILES=crates/zeroclaw-runtime/AGENTS.md` and `BASE_SHA=f87368a6aa53d16b0bd7411b002331a22622c2a7`; the link gate's six tests passed, and `git diff --check` passed. The merge and preserved row were independently checked. Rust/plugin suites were not rerun locally for this docs-only owned delta; #12129 supplies inherited dependency evidence. Hosted checks for the published revision must complete separately.

#### Earlier validation

The following evidence belongs to the earlier revisions named below.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the docs-links and comment-hygiene gates. `Docs Style` lints only `docs/book/src`, so it does not cover this file; markdownlint was run by hand below.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** no CI markdown lint for `crates/*/AGENTS.md` (run by hand below). No check can confirm that a row matches the code it covers or that a Core decision exists; that is this review.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

BASE_SHA=5d4b18d335 scripts/ci/docs_links_gate.sh             No added links detected in changed docs lines.
scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh crates/zeroclaw-runtime    Comment hygiene gate passed.

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** The row names every runtime path #11289 changes at `5740f15a35` (`git diff --stat` against master `5d4b18d335`: three files under `crates/zeroclaw-runtime`) and nothing else; every type, function, constructor, Fluent key, record attribute and test it names exists at that head (28 `RpcDenialReason` variants, 21 constructors, 32 constructor call sites in `src/rpc/dispatch.rs`, 14 added `rpc-auth-*` keys, and no surviving `AuthDenied::auth_required`, `AuthDenied::forbidden` or `AuthDenied { .. }` literal anywhere under `crates/`); the table still has four cells per row, the new row is the last row directly under the previous one, and the file has no em-dash. No Rust was built: no code changes.

v0.9.0 prioritizes opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in, principal isolation, schema V4 and a CLI-only build option.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Release gates are real-provider sign-in evidence; the five principal-isolation repairs (#11234, #11220, #11225, #11230, #11266, with #11198 tracked); schema V4 (#11218); and a build-time CLI-only option that omits gateway/web assets and directs dashboard users to the standard build.

Scoped dashboard chat has a November 3 go/no-go, with sign-in alone as the fallback. November 10 is the earliest target, subject to the gates, not a committed date.

Standalone zeroclaw-gw, full gateway IPC route/parity work, cross-process webhook handling and two-process desktop packaging move to v0.9.x. Channel listeners remain in core under existing documented exceptions. These deferrals do not complete the remaining gateway roadmap.

Source of truth: #7432 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432), current release allocation. Existing implementation trackers keep their detailed work. Feature acceptance, current-head review/CI, recorded placement decisions and the v0.8.7-tag hold on breaking work remain in force.

## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Five RustSec advisories dated 2026-10-29, RUSTSEC-2026-0420 to RUSTSEC-2026-0424, match Wasmtime 48.0.7 in `Cargo.lock`. Each is patched in `>=48.0.8, <49.0.0`.
  - The `Security` job's `cargo audit` step fails on every build, so `CI Required Gate` blocks every merge.
  - This raises the three Wasmtime requirements in `crates/zeroclaw-plugins/Cargo.toml` from 48.0.7 to 48.0.8, the patched release published on 2026-10-29, and updates `Cargo.lock` to match.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - `Cargo.lock` changes in 30 entries, each only in its version and checksum:
    - the 15 Wasmtime crates and the 2 Pulley crates move from 48.0.7 to 48.0.8;
    - the 13 Cranelift crates move from 0.135.7 to 0.135.8.
  - Their dependency lists don't change, and no other package moves.
  - No code changes. No advisory ignores are added or removed.
- **Blast radius:**
  - Builds with the plugin host: `plugins-wasm-runtime-only`, `plugins-wasm-cranelift` and `plugins-wasm-pulley`. That includes the standard 64-bit archives, which carry `plugins-wasm-cranelift`.
  - Default-feature builds don't compile Wasmtime.
  - Precompiled `.cwasm` plugin components built with 48.0.7 keep loading, so they need no rebuild (see "Beyond CI").
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #12128. Related #11924 (the 48.0.7 bump) and #8519 (the cargo-audit and cargo-deny scope tracker).

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw runs plugins inside Wasmtime, a WebAssembly engine. On 2026-10-29 Wasmtime published a security release that fixes five advisories against the version in our lockfile. Since then the security check fails on every pull request, and nothing can merge.

This moves Wasmtime, its compiler (Cranelift) and its interpreter (Pulley) to the fixed patch release, and changes nothing else.

Two of the five fixes are on paths a plugin can reach:
- outgoing HTTP requests, for plugins allowed to make them;
- resources passed between components.

The other three are in Wasmtime features ZeroClaw doesn't build: WASI p3 and garbage-collected types.

All five fixes are in the engine's runtime rather than in compiled plugin code. Plugins work as before, including ones shipped as a precompiled `.cwasm` file.

**Release note:** The plugin host moves to Wasmtime 48.0.8 for RUSTSEC-2026-0420 to RUSTSEC-2026-0424. Precompiled `.cwasm` plugin components built for Wasmtime 48.0.7 keep working without a rebuild.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A: this is a patch-release lockfile bump. `Security` is the check, and the plugin backend jobs build and run the plugin host against the new version.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:**
  - `Security` clears the five advisories: `cargo deny check`, then `cargo audit`.
  - The plugin backend jobs build and run the plugin host on 48.0.8:
    - `Check (plugins cranelift backend)`, `Check (plugins cranelift runtime)`, `Check (plugins pulley backend)` and `Check (plugins runtime-only backend)`;
    - `Check (plugin artifact smoke)`.

    The change to `crates/zeroclaw-plugins/Cargo.toml` selects them.
  - `Lint` runs clippy with `ci-all`, which includes `plugins-wasm-cranelift`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:**
  - No CI test loads a precompiled `.cwasm`. I checked that path by hand (below).
  - The Windows plugin tests are advisory and run only with the `ci:windows` label.
- **Commands run and tail output** (Linux x86_64, toolchain 1.98.0; cargo-audit 0.22.2 and cargo-deny 0.19.9 as the `Security` job installs them; advisory database at 2295466c4e, committed 2026-10-30 11:12 UTC and fetched 19:14 UTC):

    That's where the reachability notes in #12128 come from.

    - Both artifacts load, and they're byte-identical.
    - An artifact stamped with version `47` is refused: "Module was compiled with incompatible version '47'". So the check is live; Wasmtime 48 stamps artifacts with its major version only.

## Compatibility (required)

prs.title: fix(tools): reject send_message_to_peer to Discord external peers with an actionable error
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - `send_message_to_peer` hands any known non-agent target (an entry from a
    peer group's `external_peers`) to announcement delivery. On Discord that
    delivery posts to `/channels/{recipient}/messages`, but Discord external
    peers are user IDs, so the send fails with Discord's opaque
    `404 Unknown Channel (10003)` and the agent cannot tell what to do instead.
  - The tool now rejects that case before delivery, using configuration only:
    the target has already been validated as a configured external peer (not an
    agent alias), and the channel ref's type is `discord` (same case-insensitive
    `<type>.<alias>` split that delivery uses). No ID-syntax guessing and no
    network calls; Discord user and channel IDs are both snowflakes.
  - The error explains why (user ID vs channel/thread ID, bots cannot DM bots,
    peer groups carry no channel mapping) and what to do: post in a channel or
    thread shared with the peer and mention the peer there.
- **Scope boundary:** No new config keys, no peer → channel/thread routing, no
  DM path. Peer-agent targets (in-process delivery) and external peers on other
  channel types are unchanged. `send_via` is not changed: it resolves its
  recipient from the first `external_peers` entry through `Channel::send` in
  `zeroclaw-tools`, a separate path whose recipient semantics belong to the
  routing design discussion in #10926.
- **Blast radius:** `send_message_to_peer` calls whose target is an external
  peer on a Discord channel. Those sends could not be delivered before; they
  now fail earlier with a clearer message.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #10926 (identity vs. delivery-destination
  design; the Discord evidence for this failure is in
  https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/10926#issuecomment-6511170110).
  This PR does not resolve it.

### What this does, simply

Agents can message configured peers with `send_message_to_peer`. For a human
or bot that is not a ZeroClaw agent, the tool sends through the channel's
normal delivery, which on Discord needs a channel or thread ID. Peer lists on
Discord hold user IDs, so the message went to a "channel" that does not exist
and Discord answered with a bare 404. This PR stops that send up front and
tells the agent to talk to the peer in a shared channel or thread instead. How
peers should be routed on Discord is left to the separate design discussion.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A: the change is a pre-delivery rejection
  covered by a unit test that exercises `SendMessageToPeerTool::execute`;
  reproducing the live 404 needs a Discord bot pair.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the runtime crate's
  lib tests, clippy and fmt cover the changed file.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** no live Discord round-trip in CI.
- **Commands run and tail output:**
  - RED on master 5a51398dd with only the new execute tests applied:
    `discord_external_peer_is_rejected_before_channel_delivery ... FAILED`
    (`a Discord user target must not report delivery`: master hands the user
    ID to announcement delivery; in the unit test no live Discord handler is
    registered, so it reports success where production gets the 404).
    `non_discord_external_peer_still_reaches_delivery ... ok`.
  - GREEN, `cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- --skip tunnel::tailscale`
    on default features and again with every `tool-*`/`tools-external`
    feature: all three new tests pass and every other `send_message_to_peer`
    test passes. 5846 and 5861 passed respectively, 0 failed, 8 ignored
    (run with `umask 077`; under a group-writable umask, three `rpc::local`
    endpoint-lock tests reject the temp dir, which is unrelated to this change).
  - `cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.
  - `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `git diff --check`,
    `scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh <changed file>`: clean.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** The original failure was seen
  on one deployment: a `send_message_to_peer` call targeting a second bot's
  Discord user ID returned `404 Unknown Channel (10003)`. The new error path
  was not exercised against live Discord.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** `tunnel::tailscale` lib
  tests were skipped locally because they reconfigure the host's Tailscale
  Serve state.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
  (test IDs are synthetic)
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No (the
  error echoes the target the model itself passed, already Debug-quoted)

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes (the rejected sends could not succeed before)
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback

Low risk: `git revert <sha>`.
